Fisher's mean effect, which is technically known as the basic reproduction number, has been used as a criterion to determine the potential outbreak of an infectious disease. This concept, first introduced by Fisher in 1993, suggests that an infectious disease will spread if its mean effect exceeds one and will not spread if its mean effect is less than one. This mean effect criterion, which has become a widely accepted principle in epidemiology, lacks, however, a formal proof of its validity. Various researchers have attempted to provide a basis for this principle, but so far, these attempts have failed to provide a definitive proof. This article aims to provide a definitive explanation of the non-occurrence of an infectious disease when its mean effect is less than one, under a set of well-defined assumptions. These assumptions, which are considered causal in the context of infectious disease modeling, are necessary to establish that an infectious disease will not spread in the absence of these effects. By considering these assumptions, which are essentially equivalent to specific interventions, we can demonstrate that an infectious disease will not spread in the absence of these effects, thus providing a definitive explanation of the validity of the mean effect criterion, at least within the context of susceptible-infectious-susceptible (SIS) epidemic models.

Two key aspects of efficient bipedal locomotion in humans are dynamic stability and gait symmetry. To explore how fuel assistance can improve efficiency and sturdibility in bipedal movement, we developed a simplified model of a two-legged system with thrust assistance. This model helped us investigate how fuel assistance impacts gait symmetry and stability in the presence of gait errors and fuel assistance fluctuations. Our simulations indicated that both the amount of fuel assistance and the angle at which the thrust is applied have a significant impact on system behavior. Specifically, larger amounts of fuel assistance resulted in taller steady-state gait cycles, while small amounts of fuel assistance can increase gait cycle height by up to 50%. Furthermore, the amount of fuel assistance can determine the amount of energy that needs to be added during the swing phase to maintain a periodic gait. Our model also demonstrated that both gait and thrust oscillations can lead to system instability, but careful control of the amount of thrust and its angle can expand the region of stable limit cycles. This suggests that in addition to allowing for higher and sturdier gaits, fuel assistance can potentially reduce energy consumption.

This research proposes a novel visual relocalization technique based on 3D surfel map assumptions.  A multidimensional feature vector, derived from image and map information, is learned and matched to generate image-surfel pairs with high precision, even in the presence of significant pose discrepancies.  By converting these pairs into 6DoF poses with relation to the map, this approach enables accurate visual relocalization under complex scenarios like total illumination changes and occlusions.  Moreover, to enhance computational efficiency, we introduce a novel surfel sampling strategy informed by depth prediction, thereby reducing it by an estimated two orders of magnitude without sacrificing performance.  Our technique achieves an 80% improvement in relocalization success rate and 85 times faster computational speed over the state-of-the-art method, FGN.

The semi-supervised learning (SSL) approach leverages a combination of limited labeled data and an abundance of unlabeled data to achieve comprehensive insights into complex phenomena without incurring high annotation costs. This strategy has significant applications across various industries and scientific domains. Despite its efficiency, discrepancies can arise when different researchers use the same semi-supervised model on identical data but obtain varied results, highlighting the need for a more transparent and reliable assessment process. To address this issue, we introduce a novel framework for federated SSL that enhances model clarity and consistency even with minimal labeled data. By enabling local unlabeled data utilization and shared information exchange among clients, our framework significantly boosts federated SSL performance while safeguarding client data confidentiality. Through extensive testing on several datasets, we demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results and outperforms competing approaches by up to 10%.

To determine the effect of magnetic fields on jet production in black hole-neutron star collisions, we conducted numerical simulations of relativistic neutron star collapse. Initial simulations assumed Newtonian physics and neutron star material without any effect from magnetic fields until it was converted into hot, gas of neutron star material. These simulations revealed that initial magnetic field strength could be amplified by a factor of about 1000 in a short time, but the resulting effect on energy output depended heavily on initial field strength. However, a more comprehensive model, which accounts for general relativity, neutron star physics, and magnetic field interactions, revealed a significant increase in energy output, with a amplification factor of about 10 for initial magnetic field strength. Until the neutron star is fully collapsed into a black hole, turbulent motion and magnetic field interactions can lead to significant energy release in the form of jets. As a result, material ejected from the system can potentially be spread across hundreds of astronomical units, significantly expanding the cloud of matter around the central black hole.

The notion of distortion presented in this paper generalizes the previously established distortion for the quasi-conformal mapping boundary, as introduced by Beiglböck, Gentz, and Timar in 2013. The research also introduces a corresponding boundary theory and a related measure for quasi-conformal self-mappings of a Riemann surface, as well as a specific representation formula. Additionally, the results prove that a quasi-isometry is necessarily a distortion-isometry, and a boundary theory corresponding to this concept is also developed.

A certain type of discrete-time Markov chain, specifically one that is 'quasi-absorbing', exhibits a particular asymptotic behavior in its states. Under specific conditions for this quasi-absorbing behavior to occur in a given stochastic system, theoretical convergence to a Q-process can be demonstrated, representing a Markov process that is purely non-periodic in its nature. As an illustration of these conditions, the quasi-absorbing behavior of certain 'one-step' and 'two-step' Markov chains is shown to be directly related to the spectral properties of their transition matrices. The asymptotic convergence to the Q-process is further related to the 'one-step' and 'two-step' ergodic decompositions of these two specific types of discrete-time Markov chains.

A key property of graphene, which sets it apart from other two-dimensional materials, is its ability to be tuned optically. However, this very characteristic has made studying its interaction with light challenging. In this paper, researchers examined the interaction between electromagnetic radiation and sub-100 nm gold nanoparticles on a graphene substrate, within the tunable infrared spectrum. By monitoring the resonant scattering patterns and shifting the resonance frequencies, they were able to observe the resonance and its associated Quasi-Terahertz emission. Based on these findings, they developed a theoretical model explaining the non-radiative energy transfer between the graphene surface plasmons and the adjacent gold nanoparticles, which in turn initiate Quasi-Terahertz emission. This discovery paves the way for developing highly efficient and versatile terahertz generators and adhesion-emitting devices at room temperature.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, U.S. hospitals faced the critical challenge of managing patient flow in emergency departments.  Given that treatment capacity is limited, timely identification and diversion of non-emergency patients to outpatient settings has been crucial for ensuring emergency patients receive timely care.  Although medical advisors have provided guidance, there has been a lack of data-driven analysis on the optimal duration of emergency department triage measures.  Our study provides an data-based analysis of how intervention duration impacts emergency department operations.  We collected data from 20 U.S. hospitals and developed a advanced statistical model to understand the relationship between triage measures and department output.  The results showed that implementing triage measures for at least two days is necessary to experience improvements in emergency department operations, but extending these measures beyond four days does not yield additional benefits.  Our findings provide an quantifiable framework for hospital administrators to determine the optimal duration of triage measures in emergency departments.

This research collaboration involves a core group of scientists from diverse institutions, working together to develop tactical artificial intelligence for autonomous robot operations in the event of a disaster. The team has established a unified computational and communication framework for their tactical AI platforms, ensuring compatibility and efficiency among team members. The established framework is now being tested in a series of challenging, real-time multi-robot experiments, evaluating its performance and reliability in the field. The outcome of these tests informs the development of improved tactics and methodologies, ultimately leading to a standardized infrastructure for tactical AI collaborations.

Our investigation of how chiral magnetic effects influence the flow of particles in Pb-Pb collisions involved examining charge-dependent azimuthal correlations, specifically $\langle\cos[(h_1+h_2)\phi + h_1\psi_1 + h_2\psi_2]\rangle$, in rapidity intervals of $|y| < 0.5$ and $|y| < 1.0$. The analysis, which focused on the transverse momentum range of $2 < p_T < 12$ GeV/c, was conducted for Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}$ = 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The results revealed that the third-order harmonics $\langle \cos(3\phi + \psi_1 \rangle$ exhibited a symmetry about $p_T = p_T^*$ where $p_T^*$ was found to increase with increasing $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}$ and decreasing as $p_T$ decreased. The study found that the asymmetry in particle flow, which could be a sign of chiral magnetic effects, is largely accounted for by known phenomena such as particle mass and flow coefficients. The research found that a possible indicator of chiral magnetic effects, the asymmetry in these correlations where negative and positive-charge particles are involved, is found to be negligible and well within the margin of error for all transverse momentum ranges examined.

This study performs a comparative analysis of crowd interactions on two popular platforms, Google and Kickstarter, by collecting and examining data from online fundraising projects. The findings reveal distinct differences in crowd behavior between the two platforms, suggesting that platform-specific characteristics significantly influence interaction patterns. The study's analysis underscores the importance of understanding platform-specific dynamics for a deeper comprehension of crowd behavior.

When it comes to cyber inferences, individual organizations are vulnerable due to their limited data and detection capabilities for novel and evolving threats. To address this issue, we have developed an innovative federated learning-based framework that enables a collective analysis of potentially harmful cyber activities, thereby fostering collaboration and knowledge exchange among participating entities. This novel federated learning approach and its associated infrastructure significantly outperform a centralized deep learning model in terms of accuracy for identifying well-known network inferences and are highly effective in detecting zero Inference attacks, which have direct implications for cyber defense. As such, this collective AI-driven approach offers an optimal solution for cyber defense, allowing organizations to share and leverage their collective intelligence for enhanced protection.

Developing a robust plan for multi-point robotic manipulation is a complex challenge, especially with existing sequential approaches, as they often result in unnecessary movements and extended processing times. To address this, our study proposes a novel methodology that combines a customized sequencing method for multiple targets and a sub-optimal path planning strategy to enhance efficiency. The proposed method clusters a set of target points into distinct groups, allowing a single pick and place operation for each group, and leverages a neural network-based algorithm to determine the optimal sequencing method. Furthermore, we employ a simplified A* search method to calculate efficient paths between points, resulting in significant reductions in processing time and total movement distances when compared to a standard sequential method.

This study introduces the concept of using highly integrated silicon MOSFETs as effective voltage-controlled resistors in electric field and current management applications due to their swift response capability. A cutting-edge 300mm CMOS production line was utilized to create SiMOSFETs with dimensions of 100µm x 100µm x 5mm. These SiMOSFETs exhibit excellent performance characteristics such as high movement of charge, low levels of unintended conductance, and the ability to operate in both directions of current flow. A detailed mathematical explanation of the device's behavior has been formulated to guide the design of its driving electronics. Furthermore, the study showcases the capability of these SiMOSFETs to dynamically adjust the level of conductance within a range of 3 orders of magnitude, a feature that could be utilized in the development of reconfigurable devices and 3D devices built on top of integrated circuits.

This study examines how within-group connections impact each team's ability to synchronize, especially when parameters differ between the members of each group. We discovered that connections within a group cause its parameters to effectively blend, resulting in a distinct region where synchronized behavior occurs for each group in a plot that compares parameter discrepancies and group intragroup connections. Based on this visual representation, we can predict whether two groups can synchronize. However, we observed that actual synchronization might be more challenging than what the visual representation suggests. When parameters differ, parameters that are similar within a group tend to lock together, whereas parameters that aren't similar within a group don't necessarily result in a lack of synchronization between the groups, as predicted. Additionally, we examined how groups of oscillators that don't share parameters can still synchronize, as seen in certain brain activities.

The top video search platforms primarily feature content from select variety shows, which may lead to an overrepresentation of certain demographics and ideologies in the videos that users are exposed to, thus potentially limiting users' knowledge and views. To investigate this phenomenon, we've developed a model that simulates an interactive conversation between a video search algorithm and a diverse group of fictional characters, each representing a different preference, to provide an effective method for assessing origin variety bias. Using this modeling approach, we've successfully demonstrated the existence of origin variety bias on YouTube at the global level and across different countries, with an important implication being that video sharing sites should actively promote user-generated content to mitigate this bias.

A comprehensive examination of a Wess-Zumino scalar field theory in four-dimensional space is performed, with the goal of determining whether non-trivial Monodromy defects can exist within this field. Through the use of dispersion relations and an in-depth analysis of the scattering amplitudes of three and four-point interactions, it is proven that the Monodromy defect amplitudes must either be zero or highly constrained to specific forms. Building upon an existing bootstrap framework for non-symmetric amplitudes, an iterative method is developed to systematically disprove the possibility of non-trivial Monodromy defects in this field theory. Our research confirms a previously established result that states a four-dimensional Wess-Zumino scalar field theory can only harbor trivial Monodromy defects in which the operator is decomposed into massless particles of spin zero.

We have discovered an infinite number of sets of rational points on certain types of elliptic curves, with each set containing twelve linearly independent points. These sets are related to modular forms of a specific level and weight, and their weights and levels share a greatest common divisor of three. The size of the sets ranges from thirty-six to fifty-four, depending on a parameter n, and we have calculated over one million points on these curves for values of n up to one million. Our work builds on previous research regarding the elliptic curve $X_0(36)\left(\frac{\cdot}{3}\right)$.

This study addresses the correlation of interference experienced by a wireless device (WD) in a crowded spectrum environment, utilizing a mathematical model to quantify correlation based on the distribution and occupancy status of nearby WDs. An interference correlation matrix is developed to aid WDs in assessing their opportunities for medium access without relying on a centralized control mechanism. An iterative algorithm is created to enable WDs to adjust their packet transmission rates, thereby maintaining optimal network data rates and mean access probabilities. A packet transmission rate control algorithm is presented, allowing WDs to converge on transmission rates that satisfy the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions of the network optimization problem. A packet transmission rate of one per WD resultantly maximizes the network data rate. A packet transmission rate above one per WD may decrease or increase the network data rate, depending on the level of interference correlation, due to a trade-off between increased useful and interfering data rates.

Expanding the training dataset with reliable pseudo-labels is a popular approach for enhancing data, yet most methods rely on pre-trained node embeddings that may not be perfect or learnable GNN structures that may not be reliable with few labels. To address these issues, this research proposes a novel pseudo-labeling technique specifically designed for Graph Neural Networks with very limited labels (GLP-L). By producing more accurate node embeddings and pseudo-labels with only a small number of labels, GLP-L employs pseudo supervision from previous iterations to refine model parameters and integrate local node structures into the embedding process, thus improving the quality of the produced low-quality graph embeddings and resulting pseudo-labels. The proposed method was successfully evaluated on three benchmark datasets, where comparisons with state-of-the-art pseudo-labeling methods revealed superior performance in producing high-quality node embeddings and pseudo-labels with more accurate node classifications, even with only 5% of the labels available.

Video processing is typically expensive, but our proposed approach, PatchNet, achieves low computational cost while retaining high accuracy. By dividing videos into small segments and utilizing a database of aligned templates, we can match these parts at an individual frame level with significantly reduced memory requirements. Our approach enables the use of a 4x larger kernel and 2x higher resolution in the alignment process compared to current methods that process entire frames, which are often constrained by long training times and high computational costs. Our approach has demonstrated superior accuracy and efficiency over the current state-of-the-art video object prediction technique, PVN, when evaluated on the JFT-30k dataset. Moreover, our approach can be easily integrated with convolutional neural networks that employ patch-based approaches, which are generally cheaper than processing entire images, by simply incorporating a module to leverage the stored template database.

We modify the one-dimensional discrete-time asymmetric exclusion process by introducing $s$ TASEP single-particle update rules, which are applied at different locations along a line with a wrap-around rule and defined by injection and site-reading probabilities based on presence/absence parameters for an arbitrary sequence of $s$ distinct sites, with a focus on the effect of these parameters on system efficiency when $s=2$.

A novel wireless power transfer method based on simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) is introduced in this paper, and service quality is improved by energy self-sufficiency through an external power source. In the proposed SWIPT system, a multi-antenna base station transmits a single signal that contains both information and power to the devices. However, this is done using a power-splitting receiver, and the SWIPT system's efficiency and stability are affected by the receivers' instability and the external power source's reliability. Therefore, we propose a resource allocation strategy in the form of power control and beamforming design, and this strategy ensures the SWIPT system's stability through a linearly constrained minimum variance approach, and this solution can be implemented efficiently with low computational complexity with an $\mathcal{O}(K^2N^2)$ cost, where $K$ and $N$ are the number of users and base station antennas, respectively. In addition, we examine the effects of the external power source and the SWIPT power harvesting process on the system with simplified approximations and we show that these effects can be modeled as random variables, and this can be done with an accurate rate of $\mathcal{O}(K^2)$.

We've discovered a novel generality for SU(N) Fermi fluids in low-dimensional systems that are repulsive in nature, characterized by a specific type of interaction. This property holds not only for SU(2) and SU(N) systems with a single band, but also for SU(N) systems with multiple bands, all of which are extensively documented in the case of a single band. Our analysis reveals that these characteristics can be attributed to the symmetries of the Kramers potential, a mathematical framework that describes the system's equilibrium state. This potential is a comprehensive description of the fermions' kinetic and interaction energy, applicable to SU(N) systems with a single or multiple bands of arbitrary depth. This unified description provides a precise description of the fermions' ground state and is a precise kernel of the system's Kramers potential. This potential is a key component in the system's Kramers potential, a mathematical framework that describes the system's equilibrium state. Electromechanical systems can effectively transform electrical and mechanical energy in addition to their well-known role in converting electrical and acoustic energy. A new type of non-magnetic nonmagnetic electro- mechano-electrical circuit has been devised that operates based on the principles of electro-mechanics and electrical resonance. This system utilizes a suspended beam integrated with a capacitor to achieve electro-mechanical resonance and an inductor for electrical resonance. All fundamental energy conversion characteristics of triads can be demonstrated with this electrical circuit model, which offers distinct advantages, including ease of setup, comprehensive energy representation, and flexible experimentation. A comparative analysis of the circuit's behavior and that of an optical-mechanical system shows a direct correspondence between the optomechanical and electrical parameters. This analogy allows us to conceptually understand the workings of the optomechanical oscillator and experimentally investigate its properties in a more accessible electrical system.

Starting from the definition of Airy polynomials, as given initially by J. von Neumann and E. Stone in 1949, this study develops their connection to a particular class of symmetric beta-jack polynomials. The research provides a specific expression for this connection and proves several key properties of air polynomials, including explicit formulas and recurrence relations. The findings demonstrate that air polynomials connect to broader families of classical polynomials, such as the Legendre, Chebyshev, and Hermite polynomials. The study further reveals a local weak limit of normalized air polynomials that converges to a universal function, which in certain cases corresponds to the well-known Airy function. The research also establishes a correspondence between the normalized limit and a specific probability model, further illustrating the broader significance of air polynomials.

When autonomous wall-following robots encounter intersections, they tend to deviate from their path, making this phenomenon both a challenge and an opportunity for study in navigation research. To understand the underlying mechanisms, we employed quantitative analysis and created simplified models of the robots' behaviors. Our approach involved collecting data from a group of existing wall-following robots, analyzing their navigation algorithms, and testing their responses to a standardized intersection setup. The study revealed that most of these robots shift their paths at intersections, with their choices influenced by a combination of environmental and individual factors. To further investigate the phenomenon, we developed a basic model that accounted for the environmental and individual effects, as well as an enhanced individual-based model based on past wall-following experiences. Our analysis indicated that the environment has a limited effect on the uneven path shifts, while an explanation rooted in the accumulated wall-following history of the robots offers a more plausible explanation for their behaviors. Our initial proposal of the enhanced individual-based model, however, did not fully capture the observed patterns of path shifts, suggesting that additional research is needed to fully explain the phenomenon.

This article further develops the concepts of algebra and symmetry within 2d fermionic quantum field theory, focusing on specific types of backgrounds that support massless, inherently chiral fields. By extending the earlier works (Fock, Rothe, Weinberg 1; Reckseitz-Wagner 2), we achieve a global description of the algebra's elements, examining its representation under a specific, unitary action from the diffeomorphism group.

Our study examines the impact of image enhancement techniques on smoke detection in laparoscopic surgery videos. We introduce two novel approaches for identifying smoke, relying on either direct pixel-based similarity or the statistical analysis of pixel distributions. To validate our method, we created two modified versions of the LSV dataset, one enhanced with Gaussian blur and the other with bicubic interpolation. We compared the performance of our methods against the unmodified dataset and found that smoke detection accuracy fluctuates depending on the image enhancement applied, indicating that image manipulation can facilitate or complicate visual task completion.

Researchers investigated the behavior of a two-qubit M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate under conditions affecting its associated motional frequency. The experiment took into account the potential for distinct motional frequencies of the two ions involved, which could arise from variations in the trap's stiffness for each qubit. To better understand this scenario, a analytical model was developed to compute the fidelity of the MS gate as a function of the motional frequency disparity. The model revealed that MS gate fidelity is also influenced by unequal coupling strengths of the ions to the laser used in the SPATE technique. However, it was found that when both motional frequency and laser coupling are balanced, the two-qubit MS gate exhibits robustness. The underlying mechanism of this stability was thoroughly analyzed and the conditions that ensure frequency stability of the gate were derived. Additionally, it was discovered that robustness can be achieved when the ratio of the coupling to the blue and red detuning of the laser is consistent across the qubits, allowing for the development of M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gates less susceptible to motional frequency disparities.

To effectively analyze how templates influence the formation of polymer structures, a detailed examination of the factors affecting the structure of model templates in a specific type of material, namely the titanium dioxide, $\hbox{TiO}_2$, in its various phases is carried out via advanced computational methods. By applying ab-initio and molecular dynamics simulations to two distinct types of templates - the mineral and the pseudoparatomic models - it's discovered that the pseudoparatomic model is more suitable for a variety of material types, including the different phases of the $\hbox{TiO}_2$ material, except for the anatase phase. Furthermore, the molecular dynamics simulations are used to analyze the behavior of the pseudoparatomic model in an ionic solvent, specifically acetonitrile, at room temperature. This model is found to be in a stable state and exhibits a non-polar characteristic.

Gaussian processes (GPs) offer a versatile approach to modeling multivariate functions while preserving key functional characteristics such as smoothness and continuity. When extended to multivariate functions with interdependent components, the graphical GP model uses a Gaussian kernel and an adjacency graph to describe the relationships within the vector-valued function's output. Conversely, the functional graphical model framework combines the univariate GP model with a precision matrix that captures dependencies among a dataset's vector outputs at each input value. Although both frameworks are capable of modeling graphical multivariate functions, the conditions under which they do so are not entirely clear. This study establishes the conditions for graphical multivariate function modeling within the functional graphical model framework and compares the results with the graphical GP model. The findings show that the functional graphical model can only accurately represent graphical multivariate functions when its precision matrix is based on the kernel's derivative, a condition that typically results in the modeling of sparse or low-order relationships. This limitation suggests the graphical functional model may struggle to represent smooth and coherent multivariate functions. The implications of these findings are discussed in relation to extension opportunities and potential applications in areas such as biology, where high-coherence multivariate functions are frequently observed.

Some complex quantum algorithms exhibit repeating patterns in their circuit design, 
such as the HHL and QFT algorithms. This paper proposes a novel approach to compile 
these patterns into parallel circuits, where a processor can execute multiple gates 
simultaneously, leveraging the regular structure of the input circuits. Two main 
contribution areas are highlighted: first, a universal approach is provided to convert 
any circuit with commuting operations into an equivalent parallel form; second, this 
parallel structure approach is specifically applied to efficiently compile a class of 
decoding algorithms from the qudit surface code, significantly outperforming previous 
methods with minimal qubit usage and depth.

Our research provides average-case analysis of the strength average of order k for a type of random convex set, specifically the pth power of a unit ball in l_r. We identify and prove tail asymptotics for the distribution of these strength averages, a task previously approached via exact computation of higher moments. We then establish a general tail asymptotic pattern applicable to various random convex sets, a regime characterized by the convexity threshold, and initially, this is applied to the stated problem. We also consider a closely related problem, involving the time it takes to find k items with a specific property in a random collection, and derive average-case results for this scenario as well.

Our research focuses on analyzing the low-energy characteristics of an isolated two-layer excitonic conductor model, where interlayer particle interactions give rise to critical behavior and unique two-stage transition properties. To investigate this material's electronic properties, we developed a simplified two-site model and demonstrated its applicability through numerical calculations based on the many-body excitonic system's wave function. Using our model, we identified a initial stage transition where the material shifts from insulating behavior to emerging conductive behavior at the point of non-interacting layers. As we approach the point of non-interacting layers, we observed that the energy required to create pair-wise hole-electron fluctuations decreases, with these fluctuations becoming the dominant feature near this point. In the subsequent stage, we found that increasing the interaction strength between the layers leads to a decrease in these fluctuations, with their amplitude falling below that of single particle movements at a specific, dimension-dependent interaction threshold, where we estimate this threshold to be approximately 0.35 times a fundamental quantum energy scale. As we approach this threshold, we observed that these fluctuations nearly vanish, with conductive properties emerging as a direct result, where we characterise these properties using a power law relationship and determine two key exponents to describe these properties.

We investigate the potential of 5G radio technology for adaptive localization and tracking in dynamic environments. The environment is divided into distinct zones with differing communication qualities, and our model uses a pursuit differential algorithm to optimize the radio-based localization and tracking (RBLT) process. The first stage of RBLT employs cooperative methods to leverage inter-zone communication transfer and achieve accurate target tracking, while the second stage utilizes non-cooperative methods for autonomous zone switching. Our results indicate that this two-step approach significantly enhances overall RBLT performance, resulting in improved end-to-end communication and data transfer for autonomous systems and teams, ultimately leading to heightened system efficiency.

This study presents the results of measuring how the $W$ and $Z$ bosons produced in $W^{\pm}Z$ processes at 13 TeV polarize along their direction of motion. Analysis of 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of $W$ and $Z$ boson events, using lepton and dilepton final states respectively, is based on data collected by the ATLAS detector at CERN. Various spin states of the $W$ and $Z$ bosons are analyzed using matrix element methods, revealing that the dominant state is two longitudinally polarized bosons. Additional findings indicate differences in polarization patterns for different lepton charges in $W$ and $Z$ bosons events, with measured values agreeing with predictions from the Standard Model to within experimental error margins and within 1 to 3 standard deviations. Notably, the result for $W^{\pm}Z$ processes involving a positively charged $W$ boson shows a significant deviation from the Standard Model expectation, suggesting a potential difference of approximately two standard deviations.

The behavior of Causal Sets in the low-energy regime resembles that of a Cotton gravity model. This model's non-linearity is tied to a low-density limit of a limit-set theory of Causal Sets. Research into this low-density limit led to a Lagrangian representation, which's variation yields a Cotton-York type equation. This equation's solution indicates that fluctuations in a low-energy graviton metric meet the requirements to be set as gravitons in the Standard Model of Gravity.

Banaschewski and Halmos previously discovered a deep connection between two types of mathematical structures, specifically filters and ideals in Boolean algebras and subspaces and subspaces in projective geometries. This discovery is seen as a special case of a broader theorem by a author, which relates a certain type of ortholattice to a specific type of projective geometry. This result shows that the structures of orthomodular lattices and their associated projective geometries are closely intertwined.

We introduce a new visual representation method that displays Coq proof scripts as a sequence of intermediate goal states achieved through the application of proof terms. Our proposal builds on the idea of representing proofs as a sequence of goal states, which has been introduced by other researchers. However, we argue that a diagrammatic visualisation format offers several key benefits: enhanced clarity and readability of complex proofs, reduced navigation efforts when exploring proofs, and the ability to represent goal sequences more compactly than alternative representations. To actualise this vision, we have developed an extension of the Vectorised Sunstone Visualiser, known as coq-psv, a high-performance diagrammatic visualiser for coq-proof diagrams.

In this study, we consider $f$ as a cusp form of weight $k$ and level $\Gamma_1(N)$, affiliated with the Hecke algebra. By applying the process of analytic multiplication with $|f|^4$, we derive a precise bound for the fourth moment, stating $ \int_{4}^{T} \vert \lambda(n,f) \vert^4 q^{(k-1)/2} T \, dt \sim \sum_{q\le T} \vert \lambda(T_f,4) \vert^2 T \, dT $. This result supports the conjecture of Keating and Zhang for our specific scenario. To verify this, we consider four distinct cases of level and character, utilizing a set of $O_{k,N} (T^{1+\epsilon})$ relations from a new class of level-dependent four moment conjectures proposed by the authors in arXiv:2103.01103. By combining these cases with a prior work of the author in arXiv:2009.01538, we effectively prove the key asymptotic in Keating and Zhang's conjecture for a specific scenario. This combines with the author's prior work to determine the exact asymptotic in Keating and Zhang's conjecture for a specific scenario. Interior Point Methods (IPMs), particularly those based on Newton's method, are widely used to address convex optimization problems, including linear programming. Since IPMs rely on the convergence of an iterative method like Newton's method, a suitable termination criterion is necessary to ensure that the solution is reached within a reasonable timeframe. This study examines various termination criteria for Krylov solvers, such as LSMR, utilized to solve the linear systems in an offset-primal-dual algorithm, and discovers that the relative residual rule often leads to premature termination, whereas other options may cause unnecessary computations. To address this issue, a novel, low-cost termination criterion based on LSMR is developed and demonstrated to be both effective and suitable for the specified interior point method.

We have computed the first perturbative correction, specifically the $O(\alpha_s^3)$ term, to the singlet splitting function $A_{gq}(N)$ of the variable flavor number scheme (VFNS) in the next-to-next-to-leading order (NFLO). This calculation involves calculating the $VFNS$ splitting functions at $NFLO$ with $O(\alpha_s^2)$ accuracy in the strong coupling constant $\alpha_s$. Furthermore, in VFNS, the evolution of parton distribution functions (PDFs) in the $n_f$-flavor scheme is linked to the $n_f+1$-flavor scheme through matching conditions known as transition matrices, and these matrices are calculated at $O(\alpha_s^2)$ in the $VFNS$. Our work builds upon previously calculated nonsinglet and doublet splitting functions and the singlet splitting function in the $n_f$-flavor scheme, as well as the singly polarized splitting function $D_{gq}(N)$, to provide the value of $A_{gq}(N)$. Additionally, the polarized single flavor scheme to double flavor scheme matching matrix $A_{\bar{q}\bar{q}}(N)$ is calculated.

Although advancements in AI are inextricably linked to rapid progress in both economic and social sectors of society, this progress is accompanied by the risk of catastrophic failures in real-world applications. Current artificial intelligence (AI) failures are typically confined to virtual environments, such as self-driving cars encountering pedestrians or chatbots producing inappropriate responses. As AI becomes more integrated into our daily lives, it is crucial to address not just current failures, but also those that may arise in the future. To this end, this article advocates for the establishment of an AI Incident Repository (AIR) - a knowledge database that will facilitate researchers and practitioners to build safer AI technologies. The AIR will serve as a platform for sharing insights on AI failures, allowing for the identification of patterns and lessons to be applied to future projects. In addition, this article outlines a vision for a community-driven AI incident sharing platform, complete with a prototype demonstrating feasible features.

Our proposal for a precise renormalization group (DRG) has been formulated based on 
the principles of the gradient flow of a specific entropy function, where a key aspect 
is the non-negativity of its functional derivative. This method enables us to derive 
an optimized flow equation for a class of effective actions that accurately describe 
renormalization group trajectories. Within the DRG framework, all elements of this 
action class are considered, in contrast to the restricted subsets, like Wilsonian 
effective actions, utilized by standard renormalization group techniques. We outline 
a systematic procedure to determine the DRG flow equations from the entropy function, 
then apply these to the O(N) model in d dimensions, where a combination of weak-field 
expansion and iterative solving yields a highly accurate approximation for the dg 
dimension when d has a non-integer value and for the Nc critical exponent for N 
being a large number.

Ensuring the compliance of business processes during execution poses a significant challenge in dispute resolution. To address this, researchers have created a novel approach using hybrid process specifications that combine temporal logic and regular expressions. This approach allows for more efficient process design and easier monitoring to ensure process correctness. However, ensuring that process specifications are dispute-free remains computationally complex. To address this, developers have turned to automated methods to verify and rectify processes even when they initially contain disputes. In this paper, we apply automata theory to facilitate the automatic supervision of processes during execution. Our approach enables a specified process to be monitored in real-time, intervening only when disputes arise to maintain process correctness.

We define a new model for Proto-Setter'm, a high-level hardware description language, to give it a clear meaning. This is done by mapping the language to a term model that accurately represents computational processes and final circuit outputs. Our analysis reveals that Proto-Setter'm's context shift operator has an intricate behavior in describing programs with classical control flow. Additionally, we establish a fundamental property, the four-sound theorem, which shows that our model faithfully captures the language's structural rules, including the principle that redundant operations can be eliminated without changing the result.

The study of extreme values in random matrix theory has garnered increased attention due to its broader implications. Various models have been developed with the aim of identifying universal patterns among this theory. We contribute to this effort by examining the extreme value distribution across a broad class of Gaussian random matrix models, which can be fully controlled and computed exactly at critical points. We derive local limit theorems governing the fluctuation of largest eigenvalue or singular value across these models, which converge to either a Frechet or Gumbel type distribution upon rescaling by system size N. We analyze the critical parameters in the models and derive a local limit theorem for non-conformal Gaussian matrices, which converges to a Gumbel type distribution, and in the opposite, conformal case, which converges to a Frechet or Weibull type distribution.

The generation of dipolar pairs in an extended timeframe within a cavity, its impact on the cavity's dipolar entanglement, and its utility for observing dipolar phase relations in this timeframe are examined for bosonic particles. The system's dynamics and steady-state state functions in a specific scenario - where the cavity is highly dissipative - demonstrate an exponential decrease in phase correlation and a minimum Squeezing Value (SSV) dependent on the decay rates and coupling strength. The SSV reaches its lowest value in the long-term limit, suggesting an exponential approach to this minimum. When the decay rates are comparable across the cavity and dippers, the SSV becomes solely dependent on the coupling strength and initially reaches a minimum value that decreases with increased coupling. The SSV's lowest value also has a minimum value that decreases with increased detuning and reaches a minimum value that decreases with increased spontaneous emission.

As advancements in genome sequencing technologies accelerate, scientists are leveraging them to explore diverse and remote ecosystems, resulting in a rapidly expanding collection of genome data. Constructing genomes from short and long-read sequencing reads presents significant computational challenges, particularly when utilizing short reads within large distributed memory systems. To address this issue, researchers have developed a new approach for producing contigs using a distributed memory parallel system, which is demonstrated using the SGA contig production pipeline on real data. The study evaluates the effectiveness of this approach using both long and short reads, showing that it successfully scales up to 21,840 cores and achieves near-ideal efficiency, outperforming existing solutions in terms of speed by a factor of 1.75 on average. The proposed solution enables researchers to build high-quality genome constructions within a practical timeframe, even when working with large datasets of mixed read lengths.

A modified logistic equation, previously studied in a previous research article, is further investigated in this study to determine sufficient conditions for global asymptotic stability and global extinction associated with the logistic delay equation. The newly established results provide a supplementary foundation for comprehending logistic delay dynamics.

Compositional data analysis, hindered by the interdependence of its components and the artificial constraint of summing to a constant, presents unique challenges. Standard statistical methods developed for independent variables often fail in this context due to issues like spurious correlation and artifact effects resulting from constrained datasets. To address this, researchers have devised specialized techniques, such as rank-based correlation and geometric depth, that are suitable for compositional analysis and yield reliable results. Despite their individual merits, no single approach currently offers both reliable hypothesis testing and robust visualization for compositional data. To bridge this gap, we propose a statistical depth metric for point patterns in compositional space, derived from a reliable transformation of compositional data that mitigates collinearity and constraint issues, specifically the Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation. By integrating this metric with a reliable rank-based distance measure, we enable accurate statistical testing and visualization of compositional data, ultimately yielding satisfactory outcomes in comparison to alternative methods. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we apply it to a dataset of bee foraging behavior, comparing it with data of comparable dimensionality but without the compositional constraint. Our results show that the metric outperforms existing methods in terms of reliability and efficiency.

We develop a theoretical model for a perfect superconducting hybrid device,
composed of a 1D spin-charge entangled carrier system coupled to a BCS
superconductor, and create a master equation for the combined system's dynamics.
This model's characteristics are examined and compared to those of a perfect
quantum hybrid device previously studied in Nature Communications 5, 7611 (2013).
We identify specific distinctions and analogous features between the two systems.
This theoretical framework can serve as a perfect theoretical benchmark for
studying and analyzing the behavior of similar superconducting devices experimentally.

Investigating the properties of Germanium isotopes with neutron numbers from 38 to 52, particularly in terms of their skin thickness and radius, has been a significant area of study, especially in the context of $N$ = 40 isospin extreme $^{64}$Ge. By plotting the skin thickness against the number of neutrons, distinct patterns were observed, showing a pattern of increasing and decreasing values in a wave-like manner. Notably, this pattern indicates a significant change in the mean-square radius for even Germanium isotopes when moving towards more neutron-rich conditions. Similarly, even more neutron-rich  $^{72}$Ge was also investigated and found to exhibit a pattern in its property changes. Furthermore, a notable shift in the property changes was observed at a specific point of isospin in both even and odd-isotope series.

The development of a cutting-edge, isochronous mass spectrometry system called C-2S has revolutionized our ability to accurately measure the masses of highly unstable atomic nuclei. This innovative method, incorporating advanced techniques for precise velocity and energy measurements, has significantly expanded the range of nuclei that can be measured by our research facility's carbon ion cyclotron. This new measurement technique, known as $B\rho$-defined mass spectrometry, leverages precise magnetic and orbital field measurements, has minimized the uncertainty of mass measurements to less than 100 parts per million. As a result, it has facilitated high-precision studies on the behavior and stability of exotic nuclei near certain points of nuclear decay. This paper presents an in-depth examination of the new method, along with a demonstration of a mass measurement for a highly unstable nucleus known as $^{26}_{13}$Al. This demonstration showcases the potential of $B\rho$-defined mass spectrometry for conducting precision studies on the behavior and stability of nuclei in regions near certain points of nuclear decay.

A novel technique called Standardizing Flows has been developed to simplify and compare lattice field theories by comparing their underlying patterns and features. The method's versatility is demonstrated by its application to two lattice models: a four-dimensional $O(N)$ vector model and a three-dimensional QED$_{Q,N}$ theory. The results of this work are presented in two accompanying lattice simulation studies and are designed to be reproducible and transparent through the release of raw data and analysis tools.

We investigated the application of the CRNN+CTC architecture on the specific task of recognizing structured text, such as addresses, by capitalizing on the integration of a downstream parser that utilizes a regular expression to validate its output and enhance the overall recognition accuracy. To achieve this, we devised a novel loss function, the RE-loss, which takes into account the results of the parser when providing feedback to the CRNN+CTCT model. To test the effectiveness of our approach, we developed a new dataset of structured text consisting of library card catalog card headings from the 19th and early 20th centuries. Experimental results demonstrate that the RE-loss achieved significant improvements over a baseline model that utilizes a character-level cross-entropy loss, ultimately producing more accurate and syntactically correct output that better suits the requirements of a downstream NLP task.

This research investigates the production of top quarks at the LHC in proton-nucleus collisions using the Color-Singlet mechanism. Calculations at the parton level are performed, involving complex quark and gluon interactions, and combined with parton distribution functions for an LHC-like luminosity. Two distinct theoretical models for top quark decay widths are evaluated and compared with potential experimental data from a proton-on-nucleon collision, such as from the LHC or a fixed-target experiment like the NuSSC. Results from proton-nucleus collisions are found to exceed those achieved in proton-on-nucleon collisions, suggesting a significant advantage for the NuSSC in detecting top quark generation. Additionally, the study considers the potential use of top quark ratios to differentiate between the Color-Singlet and Color-Octet mechanisms for top quark production. A novel top quark observable, $R_{pA}$, is also examined. Color-Singlet and Color-Octet calculations predict $R_{pA}$ values of approximately 1.14 and 1.29, respectively, while proton-on-nucleon collisions yield a value of 0.999 for $R_{pA}$. This difference in $R_{pA}$ can serve as a tool to distinguish between the two mechanisms at the NuSSC in the sub-TeV energy range.

This research focuses on cross-domain text-to-SQL linguistic analysis, where human annotations for unstructured text and target SQL data are indispensable. To address this challenge, a comprehensive system, called TOSQL, has been developed, incorporating three key components: a zero-shot cross-domain textual representation model, a SQL data generation model and a target query matching model, along with an auxiliary task, task consistency prediction. Through extensive experiments on two real-world cross-domain data sets, TOSQL significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches in the cross-domain linguistic analysis task without the need for target domain SQL data. Moreover, removing the auxiliary task results in a noticeable decline in performance, underscoring its vital role in enhancing model performance and ensuring cross-domain representation learning accuracy.

This study addresses a critical problem in high-dimensional statistics: simultaneously selecting important variables and establishing robust causal relationships in complex systems with many dimensions. High-dimensional ranking problems have numerous real-world applications, such as in biology and social sciences, where individuals or items are evaluated based on various attributes. We introduce a novel approach called the ranking lasso, a extension of the well-known lasso model that allows for variable selection and regression in high-dimensional spaces. The ranking lasso involves optimizing non-convex, non-smooth loss functions, making adaptation necessary for efficiency. Our modified algorithm, raladmm, utilizes adaptive weights and a block-coordinate descent method to accelerate convergence, leveraging an efficient sieve to solve the resulting sub-problems in rank-1 systems. The performance of raladmm is evaluated in scenarios with up to 10,000 dimensions and a large number of observations, showing significant improvements over existing methods.

As knowledge of large-scale systems grows, understanding of irreversible processes has been limited to the thermodynamics of small systems, due to a lack of relevant examples in engineering applications. We have devised a versatile framework to quantify irreversibility in the large-scale thermodynamics of rapid and slow driving protocols, applicable to systems far from equilibrium. Applying this framework to the convexity of entropy production in both linear and nonlinear systems, we have identified a broad class of driving protocols that yield convex entropy generation, including a range of spin systems. Moreover, we have developed an expression for the rate of entropy generation under weak driving conditions and have experimentally verified the concept of convex entropy generation in a van der Waals magnet experiment using magnetic raman scattering and a spinning sample, thereby illustrating its relevance in the thermodynamics of large, slowly driven systems.

This position paper explores the hidden environmental effects of AI through a
two-pronged approach: Firstly, we identify and analyze the ecological
consequences of each prevalent AI technique during the training and
operation phases, focusing on issues such as data collection, processing, and
encryption. Secondly, we investigate the environmental impact of AI-driven
environmental solutions, such as energy optimization and renewable power
forecasting, to pinpoint areas where they may cause harm and to suggest
mitigation strategies. This comprehensive assessment is essential to ensure that
AI applications truly benefit the environment.

Research in prescriptive procedure monitoring has been expanding over the last two decades, yet its current state and prospects for future development are unclear. To determine the current trends in this field, a comprehensive analysis was conducted through a systematic review of over 350 scientific articles from the past forty years. The review revealed that prescriptive procedure monitoring research has been primarily driven by the need to analyze and improve real-time decision-making in complex work environments, with the majority of studies focusing on performance evaluation, anomaly detection, and support systems. The analysis also identified key themes and future directions for this field, including the importance of human-centered design, advanced technology integration, and empirical validation of monitoring systems. The results of this review provide a current state overview of prescriptive procedure monitoring and a framework for future research in this field.

This study investigates the steady-state generalized Boussinesq model, which models viscous fluids and incorporates the effect of temperature on viscosity. The research employs various optimization techniques and numerical methods, including the adjoint variable method and a meshfree Galerkin approach based on natural neighbor interpolation, coupled with a partition of unity. The use of a least-squares functional and a dual problem formulation facilitates the efficient computation of a symmetric a posteriori error functional. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed error functional and a proposed dual meshless method. Furthermore, the study presents two multigoal-focused strategies to efficiently solve the bounded a posteriori error functional: the Black-Driver method and a new a posteriori driven meshless collocation approach.

Building diverse prediction models, such as stacking ensembles, has numerous benefits. However, they come with a significant issue, particularly when dealing with large datasets. The complexity of model training, combined with the need to evaluate many candidate models, can lead to a situation where resource constraints hinder the process. The primary components contributing to this challenge are the stacking regression problem and the selection of suitable models. In our research, we focus on addressing these concerns through kernel methods which effectively address both issues. By formulating stacking as a kernel problem, we can simplify and address the general stacking issue. Furthermore, kernel model selection helps us select a smaller subset of models that adequately addresses the learning task, thereby making ensemble learning more feasible and manageable with limited resources.

The impact of partisan bias on public confidence in news sources is significant, yet its precise nature remains unclear. Researchers argue that partisan bias contributes to the polarization of media outlets, leading to a loss of public trust. Prefessional shifts, a concept describing the alignment of media content with the partisan views of journalists, provides a framework for understanding this phenomenon. A model has been developed to show how a partisan equilibrium emerges through the cumulative effects of preferential shifts, resulting in a dynamic that leads to widespread partisan bias. The analysis reveals that in a moderate to strong preference for their own party, public confidence in news sources remains limited to specific regions of this domain, with a rapid decline as preference increases, ultimately leading to a trustless public in highly partisan settings.

In a specific type of model, asymptotically level hairs on the surface of a compact star are explored using a specific equation. This type of star, with its surface composed of distinct spherical sections, features planar symmetry at its core. Our study employs various numerical strategies to analyze these stars, including an automatic integration method to solve the Einstein field equations and a shooting method to determine key parameters, such as the surface density and a parameter related to the star's internal structure. The results of this analysis are supplemented by an examination of phase diagrams, surface properties, and a comparison with observational data from neutron stars, such as their masses and radii. The findings suggest that this type of compact star, with its unique surface structure, may provide new insights into the complex properties of compact stars.

The model takes into account processes like RNA accumulation delays and nuclear and cytoplasmic transport of RNA. In 64Ni with zero proton number, there is form coexistence between spherical and deformed nuclear states. In this context, we investigate an unusual scenario where the traditional competition between these forms is replaced by their direct conversion, primarily driven by the monopole tensor interaction between the proton and neutron protons. Our investigation utilizes a systematic shell-model approach combined with mean-field models, revealing that monopole tensor effects are strongly influenced by the spatial distribution of particles and therefore cannot be disregarded in this unusual form coexistence case.

Chiral theories, characterized by an anomaly that cannot be easily resolved, serve as a gauge for the interactions within their particles. Researchers have identified and established the relationships of several chiral theories, which can be used to explore the complexities of these models. A key aspect of this research involves the development of an invariant, ensuring that results remain consistent regardless of the model's representation. Notably, an infinite set of one-dimensional Supersymmetric theories share this property, illustrating the diversity of models that achieve duality, which in turn opens up new avenues for understanding non-supersymmetric dualities.

A linear complementary set of group codes (LCGC) over a finite principal ideal field (FPID) $F$ for a given $[k,n,F]$-group code $C$ is a collection of codes $L_1,L_2,\dots,L_m$ that are subgroup codes in $C$, and satisfy the following conditions: (1) each $L_i$ is complementary to its pair $L_i^\perp$ within $C$, (2) the direct sum of $L_1,\dots,L_m$ is equal to $C$. It is shown that for any group code $C$ over a FPID $F$ with associated group $G$, a LGC exists and its dimension is at most $k(|G|/2)$. Moreover, a LGC for any FPID $F$-code $C$ can be found in time exponential with respect to $k(|G|/2))$.

Finding Maximum Product Edge (MPE) factors, as well as optimizing functions under constraints in graphical models, constitutes fundamental tasks in various graphical model optimization problems. These tasks rely on belief propagation and the simplex method, respectively. Nonetheless, these methods may become trapped in local optima and fail to yield precise solutions in more complex scenarios. To address this limitation, researchers have introduced continuous max-product optimization (C-MPE), which seems to offer a viable alternative method. To facilitate its broader adoption, a Brief Function Depiction (BFD) method is proposed, which enables a quicker and simpler implementation of C-MPE algorithms. The process involves representing functions as graphs and demonstrating the effects of Lagrange multipliers as adjustments to these graphs. The proposed method boasts greater efficiency and simplicity compared to existing solutions, which in turn makes its adoption a more realistic possibility. The proposed solution has been tested in scenarios of optimizing binary and continuous constrained variables. The research highlights the broad applicability of C-MPE algorithms in scenarios of higher complexity.

This study introduces an artificial intelligence system capable of identifying objects that are dropped by humans. By leveraging both auditory and visual cues, the proposed method capitalizes on the discrepancies between synchronous audio-visual signals during the dropping process, which occurs as these signals are generated at irregular intervals and encompass a range of temporal and spatial coordination patterns. To implement the proposed approach, individual components, such as an uneven signal detection module that utilizes mutual information analysis and a densely connected 3D convolutional network for flow map regression, are developed. Through extensive experimentation using the Dropped Objects Dataset, the effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated to be more robust and accurate when compared to other approaches.

Research has shown that a broad range of granular and colloidal materials exhibit similar behavior during sudden shifts in thickening under rapid deformation. The current research focuses on dense suspensions of irregular particles that become stiffer under rapid movement, exhibiting a distinct change in thickening behavior. To study this, researchers developed a theoretical framework, which found that there is a consistent threshold across different experiments when normalizing key variables, and also identified a specific set of parameters that govern this consistency, suggesting that one simplified scale can explain many other relevant scale in these materials.

This research paper outlines a mathematical model for analyzing electricity consumption patterns on an hourly basis during periods of power shortage. We provide and apply computer code in Excel and MATLAB to solve the model and generate illustrative graphs of electricity usage for various days within the power crisis period.

To investigate how Web search personalization affects user behavior, a controlled study was carried out with ~200 undergraduate participants, utilizing Google's search results and a laboratory-designed, personalization-free search engine prototype, called Google's Web Search with a Blank Profile (GWSP). Utilizing a 2x2 between-subjects design, the study assessed the influence of search profile presence (yes/no) and task complexity (low/high). Participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups, each performing either a simple or complex information search task, while using Google's search results. Following a 10-minute search period, participants were tested for recall and recognition of pertinent task information. Statistical analysis, conducted via ANOVA, revealed significant differences in both information search (ANOVAs on search query complexity, F(1,196)=4.25, p<0.042) and pertinent information observation (ANOVAs on question complexity, F(1,196)=4.25, p<0.042) when the search profile was active versus inactive. Conversely, no significant differences were found in either measure due to task complexity (p>0.05). These findings suggest that, while Google's search personalization facilitates more relevant task-oriented search queries, it also limits users' ability to gather a broader range of relevant task information.

Programs are a fundamental component of modern engineering engineering, and the automation of program synthesis is becoming a crucial area of study. To simplify the synthesis process, structured visual representations like structured charts and basic flow diagrams are being employed to aid in defining the required programs. Our research focuses on generating a single-line program from a simplified flow diagram graph by leveraging a neural network. This involves identifying and extracting key nodes and connections in the diagram to facilitate the synthesis process. To achieve this, we have developed and trained a Graph Recognition Convolutional Neural Network (GRCNN) that can accurately analyze and interpret flow diagrams. Our method is then evaluated using a dataset of program descriptions, graphs, and corresponding single-line C language statements, resulting in a success rate of approximately 55% for descriptions we can correctly synthesize.

The study of Earth's climate dynamics benefits from dimensional reduction techniques, which reduce the number of variables in climate models for various purposes. We provide a comprehensive review of these methods in the context of climate studies, which can also be applied to other complex systems across science. Under dimensional reduction, a complex system's key features can be captured by separating its low-dimensional, variable components from their underlying structure. Our review begins with a general introduction to dimensional reduction techniques and their related properties, followed by an examination of the spectral embedding, which uses image data spectral analysis to reveal the structure of variable components in climate systems. Next, we explore several dimensional reduction methods used in climate studies, such as those involving average dynamics, low-dimensional models of chaotic systems, and manifold learning for high-density data analysis. Finally, we offer a perspective on the future of dimensional reduction in climate research.

This study focuses on the accurate composition of gold (Au) ions at a specific stage, particularly Au IV, to understand stellar environments, and the opacity characteristics in kilonova ejecta are relevant to astronomical observations. Researchers utilized relativistic atomic codes to calculate these properties. calculations for a sequence of elements with the same number of electrons as osmium were performed, and the results indicate that these elements have distinct spectral features. Furthermore, calculations were also carried out for certain other elements, and while the accuracy of these results depends on accurate data, high-density data is crucial for modeling the ejecta of kilnovas.

Radiation therapy planning for stomach cancer uses 3D treatment volumes that are calculated based on the cancer tumor and surrounding at-risk organs like the stomach, small intestine, and diaphragm. Accurate imaging of these areas is difficult due to the movement caused by breathing and fluid within the stomach, which is often filled with air or a contrast agent, and its motion between breathing cycles. This movement can result in cancer being positioned differently in each image, which makes treatment planning complicated. Current studies focus on using the information from multiple images to create a more accurate cancer model and identify the stomach's position, which in turn improves the accuracy of treatment, but this approach is still not efficient enough. We have developed a new approach to create accurate cancer and stomach models by using a combination of the information from two low-resolution CT scans taken at different points in the breathing cycle to create one high-resolution image. This new image is then used to create accurate cancer and stomach models, which are merged to create a final cancer model that is not affected by cancer or stomach movement. This new approach was tested on twenty patients and the results show that the accuracy of the cancer and stomach models were higher than when they were created using the information from just one low-resolution image, which means that the accuracy of treatment of radiation of stomach cancer can be improved.

This research project is an exploratory study into the potential of investigating data from complex biological systems that are composed of modular and hierarchical structures. Linearity is the primary mathematical framework we are focusing on, although our considerations also extend to non-linear systems. To achieve our goals, we have developed and implemented various tools and visualizations, which we have made available in an online visualization system. Our findings and the computational tools we have created are the result of collaborations with scientists from the systems biology and synthetic biology communities, who have contributed synthetic data for our analysis.

A comprehensive analysis of 309 exoplanets with masses under 200 Earth masses and orbital periods under two years, discovered via the CORALIE and/or HARPS radial velocity method, is presented, and we examine if evidence for a desert similar to that found on Saturn's orbital counterparts exists in our dataset, and we consider possible inherent limitations that might mask such a feature, including selection biases, a model that takes into account stellar activity, and whether the "valley of fear" described by other researchers exists, and we combine theoretical predictions with our statistical findings to investigate the likelihood of discovering new planets within these systems.

Effective generation of a coherent paragraph necessitates carefully choosing which content content to incorporate and which content content to exclude, necessitating precise content access control to ensure the coherence of synthesized paragraphs.  This research addresses this challenge by formulating the task as maximizing shared information content content across all sentences within a paragraph, and employing attention mechanisms to pinpoint relevant content content for each new sentence generation, while also incorporating this attention regulation into the transformation of control content content and sentiment content content.  Experimental evaluations on three sections: paragraph expansion, text summarization, and descriptive generation confirm the proposed approach's capability to regulate attention content content effectively, ultimately enhancing generated paragraph coherence.

This Y-force, which is a non-long-range interaction, results in altered scattering patterns and cross-sections.
