In recent years, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have gained significant traction in the study of cognitive modeling. To tackle complex tasks, such as the 8-N-SAT problem, most successful cNN models have been over-parametrized, requiring extensive training data and search spaces. To address this limitation, we propose a novel learning rule that leverages sparse recurrent neural networks to simulate neurobiological learning mechanisms. By incorporating biologically plausible constraints, such as fixed architectures and negative Hebbian weight clipping, we can achieve rapid convergence in the fraction of correct trials within a fraction of the training iterations needed by standard gradient methods. This approach not only enables our models to attain high performance levels in the 8-N-SAT problem but also generalizes its solution to 6-SAT and 7-SAT variants, all of which exhibit similar quick learning patterns. Furthermore, our computational results suggest a potential link between neural sparsity and task complexity, with more complex tasks demanding sparser neural representations. This model's ability to produce task-dependent neural representations makes it suitable for future applications in neural-cognitive systems that need to solve a variety of cognitive tasks efficiently.

This work delves into a specific type of nilpotent algebra by examining its associations with the cohomology of associative algebras. To that end, a collection of equivalences has been established, allowing for the comparison of two geometric characteristics. Furthermore, a standard measure for nilpotency has been defined based on this understanding. The work also introduces various algebraic structures and provides concrete examples to illustrate the applied theory.

High-speed jets from powerful galaxy cores have been observed in distant galaxies, with associated active galactic nuclei exhibiting exceptional relativistic outflows. These phenomena are best explained by supermassive black holes. To understand the origins of these black holes, researchers must consider how the radiation from the cosmic microwave background affects the accretion process. By incorporating this factor into their models, scientists can better predict the development of these galaxies and the formation of these black holes. To address this challenge, a team of researchers developed a numerical model to describe how a supermassive black hole develops within a falling cloud of gas, taking into account both hydrodynamics and radiation from the CMB. This study reveals a previously unknown phenomenon in which relativistic jets can be triggered and sustained as long as the black hole is being fed by surrounding gas. These results are consistent across two different numerical methods used to simulate this development.

This section provides concise definitions of various Lagrangians commonly used in classical gravity theories. It also examines the implications of absolute Lorentz invariance and analyzes why, despite being well-behaved, the identified Lagrangians are ineffective in theoretical and experimental physics.

Our image registration approach  handles the specific characteristics of picture-based data, like 3D scans of teeth. image alignment using a 3D model and a corresponding image is accomplished by first extracting keypoints from both the image and 3D data. image transformation data, collected from a CT scan, is used to map the 3D point cloud to the desired view, allowing for the calculation of corresponding 2D points in the image, which can then be used to determine similarity and generate a transformation matrix. this approach's efficacy, compared to an alternative method, was assessed through the alignment of dental image pairs, with results showing that our strategy provides more accurate results, especially at higher image similarity levels.

Recent time-series photometry of SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, a binary double-degenerate system with a 40.5-minute period, reveals complex variability that varies across different wavelength bands. Using a multi-color approach, our analysis of 2014-2017 data successfully corrects for contamination and produces the first precise light curve of this system, confirming previously estimated properties. Our 2017 light curve and spectral energy distribution data enable a detailed analysis of the system's thermal and physical characteristics. Furthermore, our 2014-2017 photometric monitoring reveals multiple characteristics of the system, including one that matches the expected 40.5-minute period, and others with longer period variations, one of which matches estimates from Warner et al. (2017).

Global aggregation methods, including the median, mean, medians, and trimmed means, are frequently employed in various fields such as machine learning, statistics, and robust mean estimation to identify representative samples or outcomes. Although effective in certain contexts, these techniques lack theoretical backing in terms of effectiveness when dealing with complex distributions of high dimensions. This research reevaluates the efficiency of globally aggregated samples by applying optimal transport theory. We introduce novel concepts of optimal transport for global aggregation and theoretical constructs like optimal plans and costs. These metrics enable us to quantify distances between global aggregation samples and target distributions, thereby providing estimates of effectiveness. Specifically, we develop a novel approach to global aggregation in optimal transport and analyze its properties. This leads to the creation of a new optimal plan, upon which we derive an optimal cost. This cost serves as a limit for global aggregation sample efficiency. To achieve global aggregation samples of this cost, we require optimal transport distances to target distributions, a task we address with a novel, theoretically grounded distance metric. This metric is shown to define an optimal transport distance to target distributions and, under specific conditions, provides estimates of effectiveness for global aggregation samples. Our proposed distance metric generalizes existing distances, such as the empirical and sample $p$-Wasserstein distances, in scenarios where the target distribution possesses optimal transport properties of order $p \ge 1$.

The characteristics of galaxies hosting different types of active galactic nuclei (AGN) are examined, with a focus on how their properties vary depending on the galaxy's orientation and the type of AGN present. Researchers analyzed a large sample of nearby galaxies from the SDSS dataset, classifying them into four distinct types of AGN. They found that, although most AGN types are observed in elliptical and box-shaped galaxies, star-forming flat spiral galaxies are more commonly associated with one specific type. Galaxies with an active galactic nucleus often exhibit a more rounded shape compared to those without, and those with another specific type of AGN are particularly more elliptical. This difference is even more pronounced in galaxies that are not oriented in a specific way. No significant differences were found, however, in how another specific type of AGN is associated with galaxy orientation, nor were there any differences detected in certain galaxy features, including internal structure and star formation activity, when comparing galaxies with and without an active galactic nucleus of that type.

This paper focuses on flat Rotational surfaces with a 1-type Gauss map in the Euclidean space E^4. To begin with, it characterizes all Rotational surfaces whose Gauss maps have a pointwise 1-type in E^4. Then, it specifically categorizes the rotation surfaces, where the rotation curve is a spacelike or a timelike, into specific categories based on their geometry as minimal, semi-parallel, harmonic, or harmonic like.

This study investigates whether continuing training on monocular depth assessment tasks results in more effective generalization in a downstream deep semantic segmentation task than pre-training on classification. We discovered that classification-based pre-training yields significant improvements in our tests and found the effect to be more pronounced with datasets that closely mimic the conditions of the COCO semantic segmentation task. Furthermore, we discovered that low-resolution image input significantly amplifies the positive influence of classification pre-training.

Current high-performance text-based Timeline Model learning methods are heavily reliant on specific domains and require substantial manual input for causal structure definition, making them impractical for use across various domains. In contrast, our novel framework, TCube, can generate domain-applicable time-series storytelling without the need for manual intervention by directly learning from raw time-series data and natural language descriptions. TCube's approach is based on integrating sequential event generation with temporal structure learning, effectively bypassing the need for manual timeline model definitions. TCube achieves this by jointly learning to generate sequential event descriptions that align with the intrinsic temporal structure of time-series data, drawn from its inherent geometric characteristics. TCube outperforms existing state-of-the-art topic model and neural timeline model learning methods, while also demonstrating superior performance to fully supervised neural timeline model learning approaches in a diverse, real-world benchmark dataset from a specific domain.

The ATLAS experiment provides precise measurements of the Higgs boson's properties and
determines rare occurrences and CP violation patterns in beauty meson decays.
In terms of new physics searches, the most successful areas are measurements of
leptonic and semileptonic beauty meson decays, where results are close to
standard model predictions and have significant potential for discovering subtle
patterns of CP violation. The ATLAS experiment has achieved world-leading
accuracy in one of these assessments, the semi-leptonic $B^0_s\to\mu^+\mu^-$
decay, with a 2021 measurement. The experiment has also successfully measured the
frequent decay of $B^0_s$ mesons into a pair of dimuons at the LHC.

This research focuses on identifying new types of mildly periodic Gibbs measures for the Ising model on a Cayley tree with a branching factor of at least three. We achieve this by pinpointing specific conditions under which the system exhibits a periodic configuration with a period of one or two. Consequently, our findings expand upon existing studies in this field.

Reading Japanese text on digital devices requires accurate word segmentation, which numerous methods accomplish effectively. However, a more sophisticated form of Japanese noun extraction requires accurate word division, accurate for an entire sentence or paragraph. This task is challenging for both human and machine due to the lack of space between Japanese words and the complexity of the language. This paper presents an innovative solution to accurately segment Japanese sentences for machine reading, utilizing an extended short-term memory for sentence context and validated by the results of an open Japanese NLP competition.

This study examines the external links frequently shared by Stack Overflow users on the platform, focusing on the platform's (primarily) English-speaking community of 8.8 million members. By analyzing the external links shared by 85,000 users and 55,000 posts, this research finds that the most popular shared resource is GitHub, with 37% of the external links pointing to the site. An in-depth investigation of the comments provided by Stack Overflow users reveals that the quality and relevance of these links are key factors influencing the popularity of the resources they lead to. Additionally, the results highlight that the popularity of the shared resources is, in part, a consequence of strategic knowledge management employed by the organizations hosting them.

There has been a long-standing discrepancy between two predictions of the growth of galaxy clusters over time based on two opposing cosmological models, one incorporating dark energy and the other without it. Recent dark matter models, however, have shown that the discrepancies might be due to a lack of understanding rather than a true conflict, and could be a matter of how we categorize galaxies rather than a sign of the effectiveness of different cosmological models.

This research introduces the Climate Data Repository, an innovative platform designed to facilitate informed climate discussions. Initially, the Climate Data Repository will serve as an internal tool for our organization's climate assessments, but it is envisioned to evolve into a public facility promoting transparency in climate disclosures. By enabling a broader community to access climate data through a unified interface, the Climate Data Repository fosters meaningful climate discussions, allowing data-driven insights to inform collective decision-making processes for the Climate Action Consortium members and potentially others.

Domain adaptation issues persist in clinical NLP due to variations in language usage across different languages and versions of the same language. These differences become even more pronounced in medical records, which change with every patient and every new hire. This problem is exacerbated during major events like the COVID-19 pandemic, which significantly altered public communication. Our study addresses this challenge by developing a novel task called symptom event extraction domain generalization, where our goal is to predict patient symptoms from unseen medical texts based on training data from a different domain. To achieve this, we have created SymmELD, a substantial corpus comprising 5.8 million English symptoms extracted from 224,412 patient notes. By employing an attention-based sequence to symbol representation approach through word piece encoding and symbol encoding, SymmELD can be trained effectively for symptom event extraction. Moreover, SymmELD offers a practical solution to this challenge by intentionally ignoring domain-specific information present in the training data using an overlearning strategy. Our overlearning approach outperforms prominent domain adaptation baselines and demonstrates our method's capability to capture universal symptom representation that generalizes across various medical domains.

In the intersection of technology, urban design, and transportation, research has explored the potential of Learning Control Systems and Automatic Driving. This paper delves into the concepts of Learning Control and Automatic Driving, examining the evolution of control systems from rule-based designs to data-driven and reinforcement learning-based approaches. It offers insights into the fundamental theories of control and reinforcement learning, discussing their applications and challenges in practical settings. Furthermore, it reviews existing research on automatic driving, summarizing key findings, future prospects, and the inherent difficulties of this field.

In the domain of binary classification, we have fast-acting and efficient algorithms known as the Neural Network with Random Weights, which utilize a trick called "target projection" to quickly find solutions. However, there has been a lack of theoretical backing for these methods until now. This paper aims to theoretically support an updated version of the RWN network, a neural network that utilizes spiking neurons, in terms of its accuracy and efficiency. By employing advanced tools like coupling techniques and optimal transport theory, we have established sharp performance bounds for the RWN binary classification algorithm, confirming its high accuracy and target projection approach. Furthermore, through simulations, we have shown that the RWN can achieve better results than traditional binary classification methods while significantly reducing computational time in complex data sets, making it a promising candidate for implementation on energy-constrained edge devices.

The thermal stability of Strange Quark Stars at high temperatures in the presence of strong magnetic fields is investigated, with particular focus on their spin alignment properties. By examining the alignment of quarks within the star, we derive a modified equation of state, which is then used to plot $T-c_{s}^{2}$ diagrams for both thermal and zero-temperature conditions, allowing for a direct comparison and assessment of the impact of temperature on these stars. Additionally, we plot the impact of magnetic field strength on these diagrams, with $T-c_{s}^{2}$ diagrams at finite temperatures and strong magnetic fields showing a spin-aligned phase that is absent under zero-field conditions. This aligned phase is found to significantly impact the star's metric properties, with strong fields causing an inner and outer radius contraction, as well as an increase in mass. This contraction is found to be more pronounced at strong fields than at zero-field, with a maximal effect seen at a strong field of $10^{33}$ Gauss, with the star's mass, radius, and entropy all demonstrating sensitivity to both temperature and strong magnetic field effects.

Scientific research has greatly benefited from high-performance computing systems.
However, the resources provided by such systems are typically only available to
a select group of researchers due to their significant costs and limited capacity.
To bridge this gap, we developed Pando, a system that allows anyone to join a
research project by becoming an individual volunteer on a standard laptop or
desktop computer. Each Pando node runs as a separate process within its host
operating system and features a comprehensive set of libraries for running code
in various languages, thus providing ample resources for a diverse range of users.
Security is ensured through the use of signed certificates, protecting Pando
nodes from unauthorized access. By gathering and sharing the computational
capacity of individual volunteer nodes, Pando offers a more inclusive and
equitable platform to which every researcher can contribute, thereby enhancing
collaboration and expanding access to high-performance computing resources.

Relying on the Cauchy integral formula, various algorithms have been developed to solve eigenvalue problems for a broad class of nonlinear matrices. These methods involve computing matrix values and their corresponding divided differences, which can be costly for matrices with nontrivial structure or special properties such as symmetry and Hermitian properties. By applying minimal rational interpolation and its associated Riemann problem solution through the Schur method, we can efficiently retrieve the necessary divided differences given a set of matrices. This allows the eigenvalue solvers utilizing MIR to adapt to the special properties of the modeled objects and take advantage of existing matrix structure, thereby enhancing performance. A computational experiment is included to validate the described techniques.

The set of $\beta$-transforms of topological Markov chains has been characterized.
Lind and M\"{o}rtenson previously identified avaricious $\beta$-transforms, which are specific $\beta$-transforms of topological Markov chains with no escape rate.
However, not all $\beta$-transforms of topological Markov chains are avaricious.
To address this, we introduce the concept of intermediate $\beta$-transforms, which are specific $\beta$-transforms of topological Markov chains with a specific closed subset of positive measure but not the entire space.
A new criterion is provided to identify intermediate avaricious $\beta$-transforms, which are avaricious given the restricted space of a specific closed subset.
This leads to the conclusion that an avaricious intermediate $\beta$-transform is homeomorphically isomorphic to a shift of the avaricious avaricious $\beta$-transform.

To improve the transparency of complex machine learning models, particularly those widely used in high-risk fields, we developed a general method for creating attribution graphs from tree ensemble models. These graphs, however, often entangle feature interactions, making them hard to understand. To address this issue, we created a method to separate these interactions in the graph, starting with defining a concept of "separation" in graph theory and formulating an iterative process to extract individual feature effects. We tested this method on synthetic data, comparing it to another approach that attempts to disentangle features at the node level, and found that our method is more effective, particularly when there are many features involved in interactions.

Our - Flatee - is a novel federated learning setup that enables secure model training within various trusted environments. It allows multiple devices to initiate and participate in the process, all within their own enclave. To maintain integrity and confidentiality, Flatee utilizes a combination of threshold key exchange, homomorphic encryption, and digital signatures. This allows for fully homomorphic encryption-protected model updates and aggregated gradients to be shared across devices, maintaining their confidentiality. Additionally, Flatee supports verification of data integrity through digital signatures, ensuring that no device can be deceived by malicious updates or poisoned data. Additionally, an independent authority, referred to as the TA, manages and oversees the communication between devices, ensuring that the overall FL process remains secure and trustworthy. As a result, Flatee allows for secure collaboration between multiple devices, even if they are not trusted, as long as their specific parameters are protected and controlled by their respective authorities. Modern processors utilize complex microarchitectures with customizable features like cache and branch prediction to speed up application execution. These features can be automatically tuned using domain-specific language-based tools, yet mastering all available adjustment options is extremely time-consuming and technically demanding. To address this issue, particularly for resource-constrained embedded systems, we developed an automated system called OpEval. By AI-driven techniques and automatic operator selection from established repositories, OpEval rapidly identifies the optimal configuration for specific TinyDALI domain applications on targeted small-footprint embedded hardware. Our approach demonstrates that OpEval achieves near-optimal results with significantly less evaluation time compared to exhaustive searches, outperforming a previously developed tool for the DALI language by efficiently configuring application operators on Armv8-M and Nvidia Jetson TX1 platforms.

One key issue with microservices is the risk of abusive system calls from malicious processes, which can lead to significant performance degradation and potential security breaches. To mitigate this, kernel-level solutions typically employ real-time policy enforcement, but manually configuring such policies through time-consuming root access is impractical. Moreover, the complexity of microservices architectures makes manual policy creation through testing and analysis nearly impossible on a large scale. To tackle this problem, we introduce Timeloops, a cutting-edge As-call filter that utilizes deep reinforcement learning to automatically enforce optimal system call policies in time-sensitive microservices applications. Timeloops integrates with containerized environments like Docker and Kubernetes to seamlessly integrate the policy learning process into the ecosystem, thereby preventing abuse and maintaining high efficiency. Thorough testing with resource-intensive and security-sensitive workloads has demonstrated Timeloops' ability to outperform existing enforcement methods, outperforming even no policy and strict I/O and CPU limits.

In Tversky's work from 1973 and 1975, it was discovered that people don't always think of differences between options as lying on a simple line or circle. Instead, a more complex mathematical model was found to better explain how people perceive these differences, based on a formula first suggested by Gower in 1979 and later refined by Navarrete and Tversky in 2005. This research explored a wider range of factors that could affect human distance perception and applied a basic classification method to predict this behavior accurately within certain limits.

Our previous work in stellar dynamics focused on the distribution of stars around a central supermassive black hole, specifically the separatrix line that divides it from multiple black holes. To analyze this distribution, a key parameter was introduced, the ratio of the separatrix's radial distance to the inner region where two-body interactions with the central black hole dominate. By applying the direct N-body method, the equilibrium configuration of stars around the central black hole was studied under various separatrix radius values. Results revealed that, similarly to the configuration with a single surrounding black hole, the region of the central black hole follows a power-law density profile with a gradient of about -1.5 to -1.6, even when the separatrix radius is only about 100 times the inner radius radius. To derive an analytical expression for the density power-law exponent in terms of the new system parameter, comparisons were made between numerical simulations and the central gravitational potential of central supermassive black holes.

This paper presents a simple, introductory simulation on the application of model predictive control (MPC) in a stochastic setting. An MPC approach is proposed to determine the optimal charging and discharging schedules for an electric vehicle battery from a long-term perspective, taking into account fluctuating energy prices and unpredictable vehicle arrival and departure times. To illustrate the advantages of MPC, a simulation is conducted with both an open-loop and MPC strategies utilizing various vehicle sizes and comparing performance metrics includes evaluation of energy costs and revenue through energy sales. Notably, the MPC strategy demonstrates improved price arbitrage capabilities and enhanced revenue compared to the open-loop strategy. Furthermore, this simulation can serve as a foundation for incorporating real-time considerations and constraints into the MPC scheme.

This paper addresses the problem of recovering independent components from samples drawn uniformly from complex, high-dimensional, and possibly non-convex polyhedral domains in $\mathbb{R}^d$. To achieve this, we develop algorithms leveraging a generalized tensor method known as compressed PCA, which involves sampling a low-dimensional projection and performing PCA on the resulting compressed data. Our research provides explicit formulas for the embedding dimension required in this process, covering three scenarios based on the number of samples and dimensionality, such as when a large number of samples can be obtained, a moderate number of samples, or a limited number of samples. These results expand upon previous works in ICAs and compressed PCA by addressing more general geometric scenarios and achieving improved sample efficiency in specific scenarios.

To examine how species competition and dispersal affect stability in an ecosystem, researchers have often focused on structured environments, which can be difficult to analyze theoretically. A novel approach is presented that allows for theoretical investigation of multi-specist populations in random spatial patterns. This theory integrates ideas from optimal foraging and colonization strategies, resulting in a size-structured version of the Baerends competition model. In contrast to traditional models, our result shows that random spatial variability can destabilize populations, in part due to a positive feedback loop between population fluctuations and spatial heterogeneity. Numerical simulations demonstrate that random environmental fluctuations can give rise to complex and persistent coexistence among multiple species, even when their average conditions favor fewer than three species.

In the study of abelian quantum double models, researchers focus on regional algebras and their characteristics. To analyze these algebras, two types of von Neumann algebras are defined: tensor-embedded and tensor-regional algebras. It's demonstrated that tensor-regional algebras are more suitable for examining short-range entanglement and quantum phase transition behaviors compared to tensor-embedded algebras. A key finding is that type III regional algebras emerge only from tensor-regional algebras, while tensor-embedded algebras lead to type II. Moreover, a specific classification of tensor-regional algebras is developed. A significant observation is that a specific quantum phase transition occurs when a specific classification number, denoted as n(A), equals the spatial dimension. Additionally, it's proven that relative entropies relative to tensor-regional algebras are short-range universal, in contrast to relative entropies relative to tensor-embedded algebras, which are also discussed.

Our system, known as the magnomelectric effect, involves a magnon, phonon, and photon interacting with each other within the circuit, resulting in entangled tripartite states, manifested in correlations and asymmetries among the particles. We explored a scenario where the magnon and phonon are coupled with magnons and photons in an alternating current circuit, causing their interactions to entangle all three components, manifested in similarities and differences among the particles' properties. We demonstrated that there are conditions that allow the tripartite states to persist among the magnon, phonon, and photon components, manifested in correlations and asymmetries among the particles' properties, and that there are factors affecting the entanglement, such as coherent feedback and dissipation rates, and that optimal tuning can cause the asymmetry to persist among the components, such as the phonon and photon components, and that there are conditions that allow the tripartite states to persist among the components, such as the magnon, phonon, and photon components, and that asymptotic continuity can cause the tripartite states to persist among the components, such as the magnon, phonon, and photon components.

This study presents one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for all particle types and charges within QCD, corresponding to a specific matrix element and counter-term difference. The results were initially derived for loop masslessness and are now generalized to dimensionally-regulated QCD. The new findings build on existing one-loop data and serve a dual purpose: first, to verify a recursive relationship between higher and lower point triple-collinear splitting operators, and second, to verify a recursive relationship between higher and lower particle mass QCD splittings.

A straightforward method, or "recipe," of positive Neron Desingularization for one-dimensional local rings is presented, along with a related, simpler Neron Desingularization, which serves as an underlying framework. These findings build on Exposit. Math. 2014:1-18. Furthermore, the introduction of the local uniformization program's fundamental concepts and the concept of graded ring of functions field are also discussed.

The Indonesian archipelago's sundials are scattered landmarks that serve as historical, cultural, and scientific icons, yet their physical preservation is challenged by their exposed outdoor settings, leading to wear and tear. In an effort to address this, the Suryakala NusantarA project (SKA) aims to document the existing sundials in Indonesia by creating a comprehensive digital archive. Each sundial is meticulously mapped, mapped, and recorded in 3D, enabling the project to monitor their condition over time. By analyzing the geometry of each sundial, the project also calculates the local gnomon angle and latitude to further document their unique features.

This research explores a novel integration of Distributed Energy Delivery (D2D) with an intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) to optimize a power-efficient communication system. The study considers an access point, multiple D2D devices, an energy harvesting node and an IRS with adjustable phase shifts. To maximize energy sustainability, a non-convex subproblem is formed to jointly optimize reflectance, user device transmit power, and IRS phase shifts to maximize D2D energy harvesting. By applying change of variables technique and fractional programming with successive convex approximation, the non-convex problem is transformed into manageable subproblems which can be efficiently solved using Bregman Iterative Minimax Optimization algorithm. The results show that our proposed method yields superior performance compared to existing methods in terms of energy harvesting and reflectance efficiency.

This research paper presents a novel approach to collect spatially-resolved
flow data in two-dimensional planes using a single-hot wire anemometer, combined
with a motion control system for the probe. To validate this method's efficacy, we
performed a wind tunnel experiment where the wind direction was varied in steps
while taking measurements, and the resulting data was visualized in three ways: as
functions of time with changing wind direction, on a 2D plane based on the wind
direction and measurement count, and on a 2D plane based on the wind direction,
measurement count, and elapsed time. These visualizations demonstrate the ability
to gather flow data over a specific area with a specific resolution within a given
time frame.

The paper examines the computational complexity of evaluating logical formulas, specifically within the context of first-order logic, on structures that have linear orders and additional binary relationships that allow for inverse operations. It introduces a comprehensive classification system for the spectrum of these structures, characterized by a table of ten entries, each representing a distinct logical expression, and proves that every entry in the spectrum can be achieved within its designated category by exploring a structure's linear order, rather than its relational components. This finding addresses the first instance of a complete complexity classification for first-order logic, specifically with respect to a specific type of spectrum.

A new hardware device called the waveplate programmable phase disc (WP-PPD) has been introduced to modify the phase of electron waves in the transmission electron microscope (TEM). We examine whether this PPD can correct common wavefront distortions, including defocus, spherical aberration, and astigmatism. To correct these wavefront distortiles, the Fourier transform of the electron intensity distribution must be manipulated using convolutions. We use a model based on a four-leaved clover function to simulate a human cell and apply wave correction via synthetic electron intensity maps. We present a viable solution where the PPD can correct defocus and spherical aberration through convolution but may be impractical due to its high complexity. However, our research confirms that PPD-based correction is a feasible alternative to traditional correctors for TEM.

A function is proposed to calculate factorial numbers, addressing a limitation in existing knowledge where the value of (n+1)! cannot be determined knowing only (n)! and raising (n)! to any power fails to provide (n+1)! Furthermore, direct computation of factorials for large values of n is inefficient due to unnecessary inclusion of prime numbers that are not needed. A new approach involves calculating factorials by only including its prime factors, leveraging the theorem of unique factorization into primes for accuracy and efficiency, while also allowing the calculation of (n+1)! using only n! and its prime factors and their exponents. Additionally, the concept of dividing one factorial by another leads to Fibonacci numbers and Fibonacci ratios, allowing for efficient calculation of Fibonacci numbers without knowing all preceding Fibonacci numbers. Ultimately, this analysis leads to an assessment of the value of direct factorial computation due to its redundancy, as well as the value of directly computing all Fibonacci numbers since each Fibonacci number can be calculated knowing only its two preceding numbers. Furthermore, Fock states in quantum mechanics can be viewed as constructed using prime numbers and the theorem of unique factorization into primes.

We derive a formula for a one-way random walk within a $d$-dimensional space, where each step either increases a coordinate by 1 or leaves it unchanged. This is based on the principle that a random walk in a $d$-dimensional space can be seen as a combination of $d$ one-way random walks in a 1-dimensional space, allowing us to use combinatorial analysis. Our work also generalizes to the study of all walk positions in an $L_1$-norm ball or an $L_1$-norm sphere in a $d$-dimensional space, where we also provide recursive relationships and formulate related combinatorial problems.

This paper inquires whether the Euclidean path integral approach used in AdS black hole research in general relativity can be expanded to loop quantum gravity's generic polymer model, specifically in the context of a simple, non-charge- or mass-affected model with a single spatial dimension. We found that expanding this approach leads to novel polymer solutions that exhibit a holographic property and possess a non-singular quasinormal mode spectrum.

Recent advancements in speech synthesis have yielded impressive results, yet the generated speech often falls short when the synthesized speaker is unacquainted with the intended subject matter, resulting in a noticeable lack of authenticity. To address this limitation, we present a novel framework, MaskedDialogue, which enables speakers to generate more believable speech by masking and substituting particular words or phrases in the reference text with placeholder symbols. This process is repeated for various masking patterns, and the model is trained to produce synthetic speech based on all transformed text samples. Consequently, the speaker can reproduce these patterns and accurately reconstruct the original text, yielding a more relevant speech output. To validate MaskedDialogue, we developed a benchmark dataset and conducted comprehensive experiments, comparing our method against standard synthesis techniques and demonstrating significant improvements in both human perception of relevance and automatic evaluation of speech authenticity.

The effectiveness of future predictions from deep learning models is significantly constrained in environments with limited and fragmented data. To overcome this limitation, our proposed framework, Projection Predictive Reasoning (PPR), employs a projection of data into a latent space for more effective generalization and prediction in complex environments. Our approach leverages the structure of these hidden spaces to facilitate accurate forecasting, particularly in scenarios involving sparse data. Experimental validation in both simulated and real-world settings demonstrates the efficacy of PPR in enhancing prediction precision and generalization capabilities.

Our research centers around malicious versions of the frameworks that utilize machine learning, particularly those based on the stable diffusion model, which are used to create artificial images of victims and perpetrators in attacks known as 'deepassassins'. These attacks, called Deepassassins, capitalize on the limitations of the frameworks by posing as legitimate requests and can be executed without the need for sophisticated expertise or in-depth knowledge of the underlying machine learning models, as demonstrated in our findings.

Climate change is the most pressing threat to global security, yet its effects are not felt equally, leading some individuals to question the validity of the climate crisis narrative. Consequently, climate change has evolved into a highly contested issue, with approximately one in ten Americans failing to accept the climate crisis, a number that has been on the rise since 2009. To better understand the factors contributing to climate change denial, particularly in the social media environment, a pioneering study was conducted to identify and categorize conspiracy theories related to the climate crisis on social platforms. By analyzing approximately 140,000 Twitter messages and nearly 14,000 threads in 11 different languages, a groundbreaking study classified 11 distinct types of conspiracy theories by employing supervised machine learning techniques and by leveraging human-labeled data through crowd-sourcing. Furthermore, by employing unsupervised machine learning methods, particularly topic modeling, a set of representative topics in each conspiracy type was generated, thus providing valuable insights into the underlying structures of climate change-related conspiracy theories.

A study of shadow matter production associated with top quarks is conducted using data from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, recorded by the CMS detector at the LHC with an accumulated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. Two uncommon decay patterns of top quark pairs are examined: one where a top quark decays into a charged pion and the other where a top quark pair transforms into a muon and a neutron. Unusual arrangements of hadrons and missing energy are detected in both scenarios and compared with simulated predictions. In the absence of significant discrepancies between data and simulated results, upper limits on shadow matter production probabilities are calculated at various confidence levels across a range of masses for the intermediate scalars produced in top quark decays.

This study offers a theoretical framework for leveraging endogenous switching expressions to estimate the return on investment for fields of study. It has been observed that students who elect to study in fields of study that yield high returns tend to select treatments randomly, enabling researchers to utilize returns as an instrumental variable for estimating the impact of a student's field of study choice on their earnings. A theoretical framework has been established that incorporates unobserved heterogeneity, which influences a student's decision-making process when selecting a field of study, and demonstrates that field of study can be expressed as an instrument variable under these circumstances.

To generate high-precision antineutrons and hyperons using the super J/psi factory facility, a novel method leveraging super J/psi annihilation is introduced, resulting in an enormous yield of these particles. By implementing several measures including super J/psi factoring, trap technology, and target recycling, the rates of antineutrons and hyperons in a specific energy range can be significantly increased to the order of $10^4-10^5$/s. The feasible scientific experiments based on this approach are listed and may yield valuable insights in nuclear and particle physics research.

If the initial conditions of a hierarchical triple system include an extended molecular cloud, multiple stars can form through the collapse of distinct dense regions, resulting in a binary object and a distant star, both of which are surrounded by their own disks. In this setup, the binary and the orbiting disk around the outer star will interact and cause the binary's orbit to change, leading to the potential formation of more stars or objects within the remaining disk. However, our simulation shows that including the effect of gas in the disk around the outer star significantly alters the dynamics, leading to stable or highly unstable systems, depending on specific factors. In many cases, particularly those that start as unstable systems, we see the outer star's orbit transform into a distant, nearly circular orbit, leading to accretion of surrounding material and potential growth of the binary's total mass, ultimately validating predictions of earlier theoretical models and confirming that such systems can lead to the formation of heavier stars or objects.

The'state of the cosmos' concept is examined first, followed by an investigation of a cosmological model featuring matter and a lattice with an inherent flatness. By employing a Laplacian that is conjugated with a metric, both an effective Minkowski and de Sitter structure can be achieved. When the de Sitter metric is used with a conformal time, the Conformal Conformal Field Theory (CFT) can be in equilibrium with Hubble radiation, creating the possibility of generating fluctuations necessary for structure formation in the universe. A new, fully four-dimensional gamma matrix is constructed, which is adapted to the de Sitter space and contains an extra conformal time component, enabling the Conformal CFT to be in a four-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, which is a direct result of the inherent flatness in the lattice.

This research proposes a decoupled method for solving variational image segmentation models.
These models involve multiple non-differentiable terms and are often coupled with
image restoration processes, resulting in difficult optimization problems.
To address this challenge, we first show that certain variational image segmentation
models with non-smooth regularization can be reformulated using broken flux form.
Subsequently, we use a broken flux reformulation and mixed finite element space
to transform the problem into a mixed image reconstruction and image segmentation issue.
We demonstrate that this new formulation can be solved effectively using primal-dual
extragradient method and this step is crucial for our proposed decoupled solution.
Our approach involves two separate steps: the first addresses model reconstruction
using established image restoration techniques, while the second model cutoff problem
for variational image segmentation is solved with established methods.
The proposed method has been applied successfully to total variation, regional
activity, and ROF models, showing promising results.

Heavy spinning objects, in theory, interact with certain low-weight particles in a way that allows the spinning objects to transfer energy and momentum, increasing their rotation. Researchers have used this idea to investigate particles weighing less than $10^{-13}$ eV in the universe, utilizing observational data from massive quasars. By applying an analytical model based on the spin of the black hole, they established a range of constraints on the particles' possible mass using the observed variability and beam intensity of quasars from two different surveys. These constraints vary depending on the spin assumption, with theoretical and experimental uncertainties leading to less stringent constraints for lower spins. These research findings contribute to the ongoing effort of using quasars to further constrain the mass of ultralight bosons.

Our study introduces an open-source tool, called Brian2Loihi, that enables users to model neural models on a multi-core system using a combination of loaned and personal hardware resources for free. This emulator, powered by the Brian model simulator, simulates the neuromorphic processor Loihi's behavior, allowing users to develop and test adaptive neural algorithms adapted for the Loihi processor. By simulating neural activity, users can obtain results comparable to those achieved on the actual Loihi processor, allowing for thorough algorithm testing and development. It also allows users to gain insights into the behavior of adaptive algorithms as well as their non-adaptive counterparts, running solely on software. Users can easily integrate the Brian2Loihi tool with the Brian 2 simulator, install it via a simple package installation, and adapt their neural models to the behavior of a multi-core system, like the Loihi processor, by changing a singular line of code. As an example of its capabilities, the spintronics spiking memory PAMRAM was modeled using the Brian2Loihi tool to achieve a learning accuracy of 99.4% in a classification task and outperform a traditional backpropagation method in terms of energy consumption, while consuming only a singular chip for the entire process. Users can access the model and results through the public repository located at https://github.com/Brian2Neuroarchitecture/brian2Loihi.

This study uses magnetohydrodynamic simulations to analyze the 2013 March 2 event, which exhibited several dynamic phenomena such as microflares, type III radio bursts, and other features. The simulations, which employed the LOFAR and STEREO/SEST instruments, reveal that the evolution of the solar flares is linked to a global reconfiguration of magnetic field lines. This reconfiguration is triggered by the eruption of a magnetic flux rope, which undergoes a series of expansions and interactions. The rapid increase in the speed of the flux rope's expansion is observed, which is consistent with the observed behavior of the radio bursts. The simulations also reveal that the collapse of the flux rope leads to the formation of a turbulent region, which may be responsible for the acceleration of particles and the emission of the radio bursts. Overall, the MHD simulations provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex evolution of the solar flares, which are characterized by linked changes in source parameters, duration, and field line geometry.

To improve the range of experimental possibilities, the current vertical configuration of the magnetic optical trap has been replaced with a planar integrated version. This new version allows for easier manipulation and manipulation integration of the confined atoms. The specific implementation uses a planar magnetic field generated by a Helmholtz coil and a integrated atom chip technology, combined with standard optical tools in a 2D configuration.

The paper discusses a set of analytical equations that model the movement of a sphere of particles towards a black hole from an infinite distance. The role of the particles' rotational momentum and the sphere's finite size are in focus. It's determined that the rotational momentum can cause the sphere to break apart, resulting in an inner and an outer region. An outer region of low rotational momentum results in a single, wide peak in the particle density near the black hole. An inner region of high rotational momentum leads to two peaks in the particle density. Additionally, the finite size of the sphere can cause a peak in the particle density to occur. In an inner region, two peaks can be seen, while an outer region leads to only one peak. Moreover, the movement of the sphere towards the black hole is delayed due to the rotational momentum, while its movement is accelerated due to the finite sphere size.

A key aspect of Casimir interaction research is the inuence of movement on atomic excitation and corresponding emission within the framework of quantum electrodynamics. The excitation of an atom near a flat infinite mirror leads to the conversion of kinetic energy into electromagnetic energy. Klymko and Kotsaris previously found that an atom moving perpendicular to a spherical cavity can become excited at a specific resonance frequency of the cavity, and this effect also occurs when the atom moves along the axis of the sphere, but in doing so, it absorbs the zero-point energy of the sphere's electromagnetic field. The current study revisits these findings for the case of an atom moving perpendicular to a slender mirror and determines the excitation and emission rates as functions of the atom's movement, distance from the mirror, coupling strength, and wave properties. The results show that the excitation rate can be positive, indicating an conversion of the atom's kinetic energy into electromagnetic energy, or negative, implying that the atom's absorption of fluctuating electromagnetic energy leads to increased movement. Furthermore, the transition from the vacuum buffer region to the buffer of the sphere reveals diverse buffer regimes, characterized by different Em fields dominating the interaction.

Recent observations from Maunakea and La Silla telescopes have revealed 10 stellar objects within the Westerlund 2 area, exhibiting extremely high temperatures and large radii. Although these objects share similar characteristics, they differ from the young stars typically found within cluster 47 Tucanae. Detailed analysis through the Maunakea and La Silla telescopes has provided precise measurements for these stars, including their temperatures, luminosity, and radius. Notably, the stars exhibit radii up to 1700 solar radii, significantly larger than young stars typically found within cluster 47 Tucanae. The discovery has sparked a debate on the possible evolutionary paths of these stars, with the main hypotheses being the existence of unusual low-density stars with inflated radii, stars undergoing post-red giant phase and experiencing mass ejection, or stars in the stage of transition from red giant to blue supergiant. The current data does not definitively confirm any of these evolutionary paths, leaving the true evolutionary path of these stars a topic of ongoing research and debate.

The existence of this solution is established based on the mountain pass theorem and concave-convex condition.

Deep learning has significantly advanced handwritten document digitization, yet the limited availability of annotated data poses a major obstacle to further progress. This study introduces a novel unsupervised approach using Generative Adversarial Networks to enhance degraded document images, eliminating the need for expensive annotation. The proposed method employs domain-adversarial training to achieve domain-invariant features, enabling it to pad out noise and restore damaged regions, resulting in improved digitization of handwritten documents without requiring annotation. Extensive experiments, involving both handwritten and machine-printed document images, have demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed technique, with results that highlight its unique capability in handling complex writing systems. The proposed approach, with its ability to produce high-quality digitized content, has a wide range of applications in preserving and accessing valuable historical and cultural materials.

The increasing availability of digital information is a double-edged sword, as it facilitates data acquisition but also results in an overwhelming amount of data, making manual extraction impractical. To mitigate this issue, organizations increasingly rely on Item Extraction techniques, which automatically obtain digital information from various sources, including ID documents. However, existing ID document extraction methods often fail to accurately interpret handwritten or poorly scanned text. To mitigate this limitation, we have developed a custom ID document extraction system for Indonesian passports and driving licenses, utilizing a combination of NLP and post-analysis to accurately interpret the extracted text. To validate our system, we conducted a comprehensive experiment and achieved a 90.4% accuracy in ID document extraction.

Channel estimation is an essential aspect of wireless communication, heavily influenced by the design choices made in the receiver. While IEEE 802.11p channel estimation techniques channel estimation is known for their simplicity and ease of implementation, they often struggle to deliver reliable performance in the harsh conditions of vehicular environments. To address this limitation, our study delves into an enhancement of the IEEE 802.11p channel estimation technique, leveraging the predictive capabilities of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, which have demonstrated remarkable accuracy in various machine learning tasks. To mitigate the high computational cost associated with LSTM-based methods, we developed a temporal smoothing technique, which was integrated into our optimized model. The experimental results indicate that our modified method yields a 3 dB improvement over the IEEE 802.11p channel estimation technique and on par performance with deep learning approaches, all the while achieving a substantial reduction in channel estimation complexity, which was a key objective of this research.

The process of adding color to astronomical images is both labor-intensive and highly technical work. In order to develop a more advanced and efficient model for this task, we utilized Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to create a framework that can automatically increase the resolution of black-and-white astronomical images while adding color. This model was trained using corresponding multi-wavelength images of galaxies, and was able to produce accurate colors and improve image resolution up to a factor of four. When compared to a simpler model that simply up-sampled images, our approach yielded a significant improvement in visual quality and accuracy, and was evaluated as superior through statistical analysis.

Optimizing global parameters of deep neural networks is a difficult task, 
especially for networks with high universality that on average require many local 
optimization steps. This optimization problem is even more complex when dealing with networks that have complex and disjoint function landscapes. In order to simplify this optimization issue, our study proposes a new method for defining neural networks that do not need gradient-based optimization for their universal functions. This method utilizes the set of all possible universal function values as its foundation. A simpler, gradient-free way of measuring similarity between universal functions has been proposed, which our theory of neural structure builds on to define a set of unique function values for non-optimized networks. Our method's effectiveness has been demonstrated through its successful application to solving the XOR problem without the need for any gradient optimization. In order to facilitate the design of networks that do not need global parameter optimization, our study presents the concept of neural structure-based optimization, which allows for the adjustment of network architecture to better fit a given learning task.
