Equalitarian access to quantum technologies will be crucial for creating widely usable quantum-based devices and networks, especially those involving photons. An emerging technology called the dual metastructure has been proposed to achieve this, yet its connection to the line-defect structure used in photonic crystals needs more in-depth analysis. This study thoroughly examines the relationship between the two structures by developing a comprehensive model for photonic crystals and dual metastructures, which leads to an approximation method for line-defect structures using two interpenetring photonic structures. Through both theoretical and experimental means, it is shown that the two structures are line-adaptive, allowing previously calculated eigenfrequencies to predict line-defect eigenfrequencies within an acceptable margin of error. This line-adaptive, high-precision approach enables more efficient design of line-defect-based devices. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the line-defect structure can achieve guided line waves, which are not only immune to back-scattering but also prevent radiation leakage. This is achieved by combining an aperiodic line defect with a dual metastructure and using both Tamm and bound states for respective ends, resulting in a fully guided line wave state, which has been experimentally verified. The line-defined structure offers a new pathway for creating quantum-safe and secure communication channels for photonic qubits.

In the field of multi-agent learning and collaborative robots, there has been a significant surge of research in the last decade, driven by advancements in deep learning, albeit with limited accessibility for researchers due to complex AI frameworks, resulting in " AI silos." To address this issue, there is a need for a more transparent and customizable AI framework that facilitates the development of cognitive capabilities in collaborative robots. This paper presents an innovative, extensible and transparent framework, named Extensible Cognitive AI Framework (ECIF), designed to simulate complex collaborative tasks between humans and robots. ECIF integrates theoretical models of cognitive processes, such as planning, attention, and communication, and utilizes Bayesian inference and probabilistic graphical models to model collaborative tasks. The framework's graphical model representation enables the use of efficient, established algorithms to solve complex inference problems. Furthermore, ECIF's modular design allows for the seamless integration of theoretical cognitive models, as exemplified by its successful application to attention, planning, and communication in previous studies. The framework's graphical model-based approach unifies these cognitive models and provides efficient solutions to attention, planning, and communication issues through message passing and message aggregation.

Average deviation or distance metrics are often utilized in statistical research for diverse purposes, such as assessing dispersion or even estimating a central tendency like the mean. In this paper, we investigate nonparametric estimates of the average absolute deviation (AAD) around the median for independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data. We propose two such estimates - a naive one, which has a bias, and a bias-reduced version, which aims to mitigate estimation bias. Under the assumption that the underlying distribution has finite variance, we demonstrate the consistency of both estimates and establish the asymptotic normality of both estimates as well as the difference between them. Moreover, this difference between estimates can be utilized to construct hypothesis tests for symmetry about the median. We also show that the bias-reduced estimator is indeed less biased than the naive estimator and is more efficient than it. Finally, we carry out simulation tests to evaluate the finite sample performance of both AAD estimates and also propose a test for symmetry about the median using the difference between these estimates.

This research enhances relation extraction capabilities to keep pace with deep learning-driven approaches.
We propose a two-phase method beginning with extracting probable connections from a knowledge graph for an input statement, utilizing knowledge graph link prediction.
Next, annotating statement components with these predicted relationships boosts the accuracy of identifying statement-to-entity connections.
Experimental validation using the Wikidata dataset has demonstrated the efficacy of this method under various configurations.

A anisotropic momentum distribution within a quark-gluon plasma, caused by the expansion of a high-energy nuclear collision, influences how bound quarkonium states form and decay. To understand this process, researchers have developed an eight-vertex interaction that describes the fragmentation of a quark into a meson consisting of a quark and an antiquark, and used this to calculate the fragmentation characteristics of various quarkonium states in an anisotropic QCD medium with a specific type of mass that changes as the environment becomes more dense in the early stages of nuclear collisions. This research also takes into account the effects of the anisotropy and density on the quarkonium states' mass and momentum distribution.

Our investigation of Tb3RuO7 reveals the magnetic configuration of Tb3RuO7 with an atypical internal magnetic field that significantly impacts the spin-orbit coupling of Ru and hinders the internal field's uniform distribution, particularly due to a weakened interlayer interdependence near a Ru plane. By applying a moderate magnetic field applied along the interlayer axis, we observe disordered behavior above 2 T, marked by the appearance of magnetic components perpendicular to the interlayer plane and enhanced magnetic fluctuations detected through neutron scattering experiments. This disordered state exhibits similarities to other multiferroic compounds, underlining the significance of the nonuniform internal magnetic field in driving it.

In complex systems like the brain, communication can change based on past interactions and temporal patterns, making traditional learning models inadequate for deciphering dynamic time-series data. Our novel framework generates a distinctive representation of localized time-series data for machine learning applications by producing modulated recurrent activations that capture both past and concurrent information. This novel representation is evidence-based, ensuring it directly correlates with how effectively downstream models perform. Our method has been successfully applied to predict epileptic seizures and directions of disease progression in MRI scans, outperforming or matching the latest methods in these domains. Moreover, our model excels at generalizing to new data not seen during training, a capability rarely achieved by alternative models.

Current methods in machine learning are largely based on finding similarities and patterns in data, but they struggle with unforeseen circumstances and complex relationships between variables. To address this limitation, a new approach is introduced that takes a semi-generative perspective on modeling, aiming to generate complete data while considering both its observable and unobservable aspects. This method enables machines to make more accurate predictions in novel situations and has been theoretically proven to find the minimum risk required for optimal performance. To put this concept into practice, a novel semi-generative loss function is proposed, and efficient algorithms are developed to implement it, including one for making predictions and another for adjusting distribution shifts that only become apparent after analysis. These algorithms demonstrate better or equal performance when compared to existing techniques that deal with distribution shifts.

This comprehensive monograph delves into the theoretical underpinnings of deep learning architectures, drawing from advanced mathematical and theoretical concepts. The target audience consists of researchers and scholars in the fields of applied mathematics, statistical physics, and theoretical machine learning. The monograph is designed to serve as a foundational reference, bridging existing knowledge and presenting key findings from recent progressive research in a coherent and accessible manner. Each chapter focuses on distinct topics, starting with an in-depth introduction to the subjects at hand, followed by a detailed exploration of key issues and challenges. The monograph's uniform structure and thorough treatment of each topic make it an indispensable resource for entering the deep learning research landscape.

In the context of harmonic analysis on the half of a Lie group, I have a specific area of interest - one that focuses on the behavior of matrix coefficients associated with irreducible unitary representations, particularly regarding their decay properties at the boundary. This interest is driven by a fundamental question regarding the existence of a dominant factor in the decay of these coefficients. It turns out that this question can be equivalently formulated as an inquiry about geometric minima of a half group. By applying a group geometric approach, I am able to identify the dominant factor in the decay of matrix coefficients for a wide range of half groups, including those associated with quasi and reductive Lie groups. Moreover, I am also in a position to refine and establish geometric minima for spherical functions and an associated class of Bessel functions.

In this research, we investigate the capability of DL-based jet classifiers to utilize variables that are both expert-defined and interpretable. To illustrate, we compare a range of popular jet taggers, including rDNN, rDNNN, and rDNNN+GIN, with a combination of DL taggers (rDNNN and rDNNN+GIN) and leading-order Parton Shower hadronic tau taggers. By employing the Layer-wise Relevance Propagation algorithm, we investigate the role of the data it is trained on, as well as the impact of pre-training on data set, on the performance of rDNNN and rDNNN+GIN. Additionally, we show that rDNNN and rDNNN+GIN exhibit an affinity to jet substructure features that are commonly found in signal jets, such as missing cone activity and unequal angular momentum distributions.

This research introduces a generalization of r-linked Stirling numbers of the second kind, called degenerate r-linked Stirling numbers. These numbers serve as a unified framework extending r-degenerate Bell numbers and r-linked Stirling numbers. The generalized numbers have associated generating functions and satisfy recursive relationships. Furthermore, this study provides identity formulas for partial ordinary and exponential sums involving the generalized numbers. The results obtained extend previous findings in combinatorial mathematics.

In the field of group representation theory, four types of organized group representations are commonly studied: single ordinary, single gray, double ordinary, and double gray. These representations can be broken down into irreducible components, and a method exists to compute them using the Gray code. Another approach employs a set of polynomials based on Chebyshev and Hermite to find these irreducible components. This work extends to determining location symmetry induced representations, and provides explicit location invariant location symmetry induced irreducible components for double gray organization representations based on the characters of these representations.

In this research study, specific vector fields, specifically Killing vector fields, have been identified and expressed in terms of coordinates for algebraic varieties defined by equations, which are a subset of the n-dimensional space. These variety definitions involve polynomials and have a particular type of vector field as a root, characterized as geometric. The corresponding paths of these vector fields can be calculated using geometric methods and their directions have a meaningful interpretation within the context of the manifold associated with these varieties. Building upon established theories, the research demonstrates that a certain type of impulse operator can be applied, specifically for Killing vector fields on geodesic paths, and this application has significant ramifications within the field of control theory. As part of the research, a control system was designed and implemented for a specific model of a double geodesic beam and various strategies for controlling the beam were analyzed.

The sign problem, a well-documented challenge in quantum Monte Carlo calculations for fermions, can make obtaining accurate results extremely difficult or impossible due to noise scaling with 1/M and negative weights. Recent advancements employing machine learning have offered potential solutions by training neural networks to replace sign functions, reducing noise to 1/M^2. Our research reveals that complex numbers can effectively tackle the sign problem on fermionic Hamiltonians without prior training. Using a simple phase factor as the imaginary part of the weight matrix mimics a phase factor update for each sample, providing significant performance gains and making the method applicable to systems that also face long-time difficulties.

A trilinear interaction between two composite states and one fundamental particle, known as a "Flavon" $\phi$, which acquires mass through its condensation with the Higgs field, leads to unique predictions of non-standard interactions and non-standard self-couplings of the Higgs field. The research investigates the theoretical foundations of these composite Flavon-Higgs models and their associated non-linear realization, resulting in distinct non-standard self-couplings of the Higgs field with coupling ratios $\lambda_3 v^2/\lambda_2 v^2 = \lambda_3 v/\lambda_2 = 2 \pm O(m_{\phi}/v)$ and $\lambda_4 v^3/\lambda_2 v^2 = m_{\phi} m_{\phi'} v/\lambda_2, \dots$. Here $\lambda_n$ represents the Lagrangian coefficient of a dimension-$n$ operator and $m_{\phi}$ is the mass of a heavy composite state. The non-standard self-couplings of the Higgs field present distinct signatures, characterized by ratios deviating from unity, which could be observed experimentally. The ratios' values are directly proportional to the masses of the heavy composite states, and their signs can serve as a definitive indicator of the underlying non-linear composite model structure.

Research in various fields such as performance, learning and perception has utilized the concept of 'shadow awareness', where people perform complex actions while observing a simplified version of their surroundings. Studies have shown that coexisting with a different view of the environment can impact high-level planning. We investigated shadow perception and its influence on performance in a VR setting. Participants interacted with a virtual room through an HMD and a secondary HMD, while also seeing a darkened version, or 'shadow', of the environment on the primary HMD. Our experiments on perception and location estimation along with tasks of landing and navigation revealed that users adapted their strategies based on combining information from both HMDs. Surprisingly, the presence of the shadow aspect did not significantly decrease overall performance but did affect performance metrics, such as the location estimation task showing that participants were more accurate with the darkened version and performed an average of 20.4% below the Weber-Law prediction in the primary HMD.

To address language inequality in NLP, a large, pre-trained language model called BigScience was developed in collaboration with HuggingFace and 46,000 contributors on the Medium platform. The model, known as BERT-WF and trained on 103 languages, aims to provide a comprehensive, high-quality dataset for each language. However, its reliance on media content may not effectively cover languages that are less represented online, such as African languages. In this study, we explore whether BERT-WF's cross-lingual capabilities can be improved by modifying its architecture, specifically by introducing more relevant data and a multi-task approach that includes data from a broader range of sources like Wikipedia and social media platforms.

When a core formed in star birth starts to break apart, it forms a binary system, consisting of two stars orbiting each other. The mass of these stars is affected by the mass and spin of the parent core. Using computer models, researchers studied what happens when a core with a mass of 1 to 3 solar masses and a certain amount of spin breaks apart. They found that in most cases, a binary system is formed, consisting of two stars orbiting each other, with a certain amount of mass and angular momentum. This mass and spin is affected by the mass to the power of 1.15 times a certain factor.

This research introduces a rapid method for separating mixed signals in Independent Component Analysis (ICA), which involves exploiting a quick approximation of ICA's objective function by initially converting it into a polynomial with a fixed number of terms and then applying a Newton-type optimization approach. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this technique significantly reduces ICA's computational expenses by at least an order of magnitude, making it feasible to utilize ICA in real-time applications on resource-constrained devices. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed approach, a set of 12 ICA datasets was utilized to evaluate its performance in terms of separation quality and speed requirements.

We have obtained proof of a conjecture from prior research, which asserts that 3-coloring specific families of tripartite graphs is an task for the Stochastic Calculus (PCT) but can't be proven in a extended polynomial calculus (PC*) with low polynomial complexity. We also demonstrate the inequality of two limited logics when it comes to handling the satisfiability of certain formulas in polynomial time.

A local ring is classified as a sigma-elementary local ring if its associated sigma-spectrum contains only finitely many prime ideals, where the sigma-spectrum is defined by the set of prime ideals I such that the local ring's localization at any prime ideal I is contained in I. In a finite-dimensional complete topological algebra over a topological field K with the discrete topology, we show that the associated sigma-spectrum of a given prime ideal I is defined by the localizations of its associated topological algebra, and the sigma-spectrum of the topological algebra equals the local spectrum of its maximal ideal, which can be defined as the set of prime ideals I that are contained in the maximal ideal of the topological algebra and defined as the set of prime ideals I that are strictly contained in the maximal ideal. We construct an infinite family of complete topological algebras, consisting of a subclass of equidimensional and equidimensional-free topological algebras, such that the local spectrum of their maximal ideal consists of a countably infinite set of maximal ideals.

In assertion checking, the 'uncheckable assertion' issue arises when an error exists but no test case can be found to expose it, leading to unvalidatable assertions. This problem is particularly prevalent in industry, with some sources estimating it accounts for up to 30% of all assertions. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods to increase the effectiveness of assertion checking by developing techniques to find uncheckable cases and potentially improve their test coverage. One such approach utilizes a framework-based strategy to generate frameworks that can significantly increase the number of checkable assertions. This thesis delves into the framework method's applicability in assertion checking to ultimately enhance the detectability of errors.

Identifying traffic incidents accurately and instantly is a crucial aspect of intelligent incident management systems, as it directly impacts public safety and transportation efficiency. To achieve real-time accuracy, researchers have turned their attention to social media platforms like Twitter, which offer vast amounts of geotagged data that can be leveraged for incident detection. However, accurately pinpointing the location and time of incidents remains a significant challenge due to the imprecise nature of social media posts. To overcome this limitation, this study proposes a sophisticated incident detection system that utilizes a hierarchical hidden Markov model to identify social media incidents with high temporal and spatial precision. By incorporating a timeseries module and a spatial module, the proposed system effectively captures the evolution of incident-related topics over time and geospatial proximity patterns. Through rigorous simulations on a real dataset of Twitter posts, the proposed system has demonstrated superior performance, outperforming existing incident detection systems in both temporal and spatial accuracy.

Galaxy map distortions can hide crucial information about how galaxies are related, which is often studied using the cosmic bispectrum of galaxy density and matter radiation fluctuations. A new approach facilitates faster analysis of these effects by allowing researchers to calculate the galaxy bias, B-mode, and an estimator of the fiducial cosmology's B-mode coefficient using the three-dimensional CMB and galaxy maps' pixel data, which can significantly decrease computation times by a factor of up to $10^6$. We verify our algorithm by testing it with various distortion methods and cross-check with existing simulation tools and theoretical models, finding our approach produces results within 1% of standard approaches for linear galaxy models and within a few percent for nonlinear galaxy models.

By integrating Bayesian learning within a game-theoretic framework, we develop an efficient algorithm that significantly reduces the testing burden for neural network classifiers, specifically in the case of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). Our approach involves applying variational inference with neural network approximators, followed by solving a convex optimization problem to obtain certifiable robustness on a small dataset. This method showcases improved test-time efficiency and overcomes a problem known as BNN collapse, enabling BNNs to reach accuracy rates comparable to deterministic neural networks while providing formal accuracy guarantees.

In recent years, online rumors spread rapidly on social media, hindering public health safety and social stability. In this study, Chinese government press releases related to COVID-19 from January to March 2020 were analyzed to understand the dynamics of rumor dissemination. By examining key events, such as epidemic outbreak, quarantine measures, and virus spread in different regions, we developed a general model that can be easily adapted to various cases of information dissemination. This model enables a straightforward, quantitative method for predicting rumor lifespan and detecting abnormal patterns that may indicate external interference affecting information spread. Our findings, when applied to different contexts, demonstrate that sojourn time and pressure from higher authorities can accurately predict observed rumor behavior. Moreover, we identified significant differences in Chinese government communication strategies that had a notable impact on the dissemination of COVID-19 rumors. Our study provides a thorough understanding of rumor dissemination mechanisms and offers a reliable approach for evaluating the effectiveness of intervention strategies to combat online misinformation.

This study investigates the impact of reducing spectral dimensionality in hyperspectral image classification. We constructed datasets of varying spectral dimensions and examined their effects on both supervised and unsupervised learning methods. The research is conducted on the Pavia University, Salinas, and Pavia Center images and utilizes the Information Bottleneck principle to lower spectral dimensions. The findings demonstrate that even a substantial reduction in spectral dimensions can substantially degrade classification performance, particularly for narrow narrowband and discontinuous spectral curves. Moreover, we observed distinct patterns of dimensionality-induced classification behavior among different targets due to variations in spectral profiles. The study underscores the significance of spectral dimensionality in hyperspectral image classification and emphasizes the need for further theoretical exploration and practical evaluation.

We introduce a method to create a compact, self-contained version of GPT-2 language models that naturally captures the models' original predictions as well as its internal thought processes. This model's behavior is analyzed in two main areas: its representation of word meanings and the accuracy of intermediate processing steps in predicting subsequent text. Our evaluation also examines how our model compares to other models in the same family and its ability to handle tasks that require understanding text naturally, such as answering questions and doing various tasks automatically. Our results show that the model's size can be reduced with only a small decrease in accuracy, a property not seen in other models. Additionally, we found that the model's internal processing closely relates to its external predictions, a finding that reveals more about its behavior. Our work is the first to explore the relationship between intermediate processing and external predictions in language models, expanding our understanding of their behavior.

Two innovative techniques, PROK and CEK, have been developed to efficiently validate and improve protein structure models by leveraging amide proton chemical shifts through quantum mechanical calculations and comparison with experimental data. The PROK method provides rapid, high-accuracy validation of protein structures at a low computational cost of O(N) by focusing on protein surface residues. The techniques have demonstrated strong correlation between computed and experimental values of $^{15}$N and $^{1}$H chemical shifts. The proposed techniques also offer an automatic protein structure optimization capability via the CEK method. The performance of CEK surpasses a top-existing tool in protein structure optimization with a lower root-mean-square error and enhanced protein surface accuracy. The exceptional performance of CEK is attributed to its utilization of an optimized, simplified potential function and a novel grid-based side chain model. The techniques have demonstrated robustness and rapid convergence, capable of validating proteins with a minimum of 30 residues and automatically optimizing the protein structure within 5-15 iterations. The exceptional performance of CEK is attributed to its utilization of a simplified potential function and a novel grid-based side chain model. The performance of CEK surpasses a top-existing tool in protein structure optimization with a lower root-mean-square error and enhanced protein surface accuracy.

Deep learning models are frequently enhanced by modifying the loss function in an attempt to accelerate training or improve final performance. This study critically examines these modifications, which are typically motivated by acceleration or a positive impact on classification accuracy, and finds that many are unfounded. To validate these loss function modifications, the researchers established a systematic evaluation framework that thoroughly investigates their effects on classification tasks. This framework involves conducting experiments on diverse networks, datasets, and loss function variations to yield comprehensive insights into suitable scenarios for each modification. The analysis also sheds light on how these loss function alterations influence training dynamics and classification outcomes, as well as their potential implications for model generalization and robustness. The findings reveal that certain loss function modifications can lead to overparameterization and poor generalization, and some are ineffective or inconsistent in optimizing network parameters. Ultimately, the researchers establish clear guidelines for when these loss function modifications are beneficial and discuss their broader implications, particularly for scenarios involving limited training data.

We develop a novel viewpoint on the nonperturbative diagrammatic approach known as the parquet theory, redefining the four-point vertex as the total interaction minus two components: a model-dependent part and a temperature-dependent part. By focusing on a divergence-free, temperature-dependent Hamiltonian operator, we show that the theory can be obtained as the stationary solutions of its associated nonlinear eigenvalue problem. This formulation simplifies the traditional approach by eliminating the need for a specific nonperturbative four-fermion model, and it can be seamlessly integrated with the existing parquet theory approach. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the traditional and new methods, and use a simple one-dimensional model to demonstrate the equivalence of the two approaches.

To effectively describe the exciton insulator state in two-dimensional layered transition metal dichalcogenides, an innovative ab initio method is proposed. This groundbreaking approach seamlessly integrates electron correlations within dynamic mean-field theory and phonon interactions, thus overcoming existing limitations in the field. Dynamic mean-field theory is implemented using the full potential linearized augmented plane wave + local orbitals code combined with maximally localized Wannier functions and atomic orbital basis sets, while exciton liquefaction is modeled using the random phase approximation including atom-specific explicit correlation terms. Phonon coupling is then accounted for using a linear combination of plane waves within the density functional perturbation theory framework, enabling seamless coupling with the first-principles wave function calculations. Dynamic self-energy corrections are derived from these phonon calculations to yield the total self-energy. This novel ab initio technique for treating exciton liquefaction is now in a state of initial implementation and has been applied to TiSe_2 to yield an accurate description of its ground state properties. Notably, our results align with recent experimental findings, revealing that exciton binding energy in TiSe_2 is influenced by phonon coupling in a way that contributes positively to it.

In recent years, digital security threats to critical systems have been rising steadily, prompting organizations to seek effective methods for managing their cybersecurity operations. Although information and communication technology (ICT) tools such as social engineering and knowledge management have been utilized to mitigate these threats, the integration of community-driven components in cybersecurity remains underexplored. This paper utilizes qualitative data from a text-based reporting system to analyze the interactions between community members and the organization's dispatching team, aiming to shed light on the vital yet understudied aspects of community-driven cybersecurity, including knowledge creation and management, trust development, and communication strategies.

This study examines the impact of nematicity on the properties of a superconducting material, with a particular focus on its symmetry, which is based on a square lattice and has a broken rotational symmetry, resulting in two distinct Fermi surfaces when it interacts with a nematic state, one for spin-up electrons and the other for spin-down electrons, resulting in two different local densities of states at the Fermi level, with a nematic susceptibility that can be measured by applying a spin magnetic field parallel to it, which causes the system to paramagnetically respond, with this paramagnetic response being more significant at lower dimensions and becoming comparable to the conventional Pauli limit at three-dimensional systems, with this analysis being carried out using both conventional and unconventional approaches to solve the equations of motion for quasiparticles near the Fermi level, with both methods yielding the same results, with this paramagnetic response being more significant at lower temperatures and certain crystal orientations, with this being particularly more significant at lower dimensions.

This paper introduces the Engaged Minimax Learner (EML), a novel minimax approach for zero-sum two-player turn-based games. The EML minimizes the maximum possible loss by ensuring its strategy is unexploitable, regardless of the opponent's actions. We propose EML as a new criterion for minimax optimality and demonstrate that it can be achieved through Nash dynamics in a finite number of steps. Furthermore, the paper examines the engaged minimax condition in the context of the game of Rock-Paper-Scissors and explores its application to deep learning.

This study examines how the musical composition of Western music has become more intricate over time by examining musical datsets spanning three centuries of music theory and performance. To measure complexity, various metrics of information theory are employed, including entropy and surprise, to analyze patterns in music at different scales from individual beats to entire compositions. To ensure accurate results, a set of data preprocessing methods is employed to eliminate the influence of extraneous factors and ensure that the chosen measures accurately reflect musical composition and performance. The research reveals that modern music is distinctly different from historical music and that there is a growing trend where music is characterized by both highly and low-probability events, leading to an increase in the apparent complexity of the musical datsets as time progresses.

A widely used approach in combinatorial search, the backtracking search heuristic, drives reinforcement-based exploration of a problem's solution space through multiple search iterations, each linked through partial solutions. A random search procedure based on partial solutions will eventually locate the optimal solution given a certain assumption about these solutions' structure; this finding supports the self-tuning adaptive memory procedure, a class of methods including adaptive memory programming and simulated annealing. For a specific problem type, it is also proven that the search procedure finds the optimal solution within finite time, a result with significant implications for optimization problems like job scheduling. Additionally, research connects this proof to adaptive memory programming and its related development, including a simpler, faster strategy variant.

This paper explores the concept of playful computation, examining how an AI's creative outputs can be influenced by a designer's playful interventions during development. Specifically, we studied the harmony between two designers and an AI in the context of the Glow game, where each designer and the AI contribute uniquely to the overall experience, creating surprising and enjoyable moments of collaboration and competition.

Reward learning in complex, loosely defined tasks is crucial for the development of robust reinforcement learning agents. However, defining exact reward functions can be a labor-intensive task for human annotators, especially when multiple options are available and each must be evaluated with equal effort. In this research, we introduce an efficient solution that leverages visual insights to group similar definition options and enables annotators to rapidly identify the best choice for each group, thus minimizing time spent per definition. Building on this concept, we propose ClusRew, a novel approach that combines cluster ranking with pre-trained image embeddings to facilitate efficient reward learning. We further enhance ClusRew by integrating model-predicted high-ranking definitions to cut down the number of required annotations in a sequential learning setting. Experimental results on defining complex tasks in visual navigation and robotic manipulation demonstrate that ClusRep achieves a 4.1 to 7.3 times speedup in reducing annotating time without impacting the final reward quality, and a proposed sampling strategy yields even better outcomes by decreasing annotations needed on difficult definition options.

This paper examines the property of core-compactness in Smyth powerdomains within the context of domain theory. It establishes that Smyth powerdomains possess the core-compact characteristic when their underlying domains are core-compact. Furthermore, it provides an equivalent definition for core-compactness in Smyth powerdomains in terms of continuous lattices and compact elements, and ultimately, it gives a criterion for core-compactness in Smyth powerdomains through compact elements.

A rotation of a vortex ring is a rarer phenomenon in 2D liquids than in 2D gases. In gases, vortex rings in 2D are highly unstable and disintegrate quickly. We find that a vortex ring in 2D liquids is highly stable and can exist for a long time. We establish the existence of a sharp vortex ring in 2D liquids with positive circulation, which is a significant outcome in 2D vertex dynamics. Our analysis shows that such vortex rings are perfectly stable and can survive for a long period of time. We demonstrate that the vortex ring will take a long time to decay into a point vortex in 2D liquids.

Recent research has utilized ensemble weather forecasting and machine learning, such as Neural Networks, in downscaling projects. The ENR-IPW method, an enhanced inverse probability weighting technique, standardizes the weights by accounting for ensemble forecasts. This study evaluates the ENR-IPW method in generating daily rainfall estimates at a regional scale, using high-resolution model simulations, observed rainfall data, and pre- and post-variables from ensemble weather models. The model's predictions are refined by adjusting for the probabilities derived from the ensemble weather models, ensuring a more reliable bias correction. The outcomes are then validated using observed rainfall data spanning the years 2005 to 2017. The analysis compares ENR-IPW to traditional inverse probability weighting (IPW) that ignores ensemble forecasts, as well as multiple-forecast averaging (MFA). The evaluation employs the continuous ranked score (CRPS) metric and demonstrates that consideration of ensemble weather model probabilities significantly improves bias correction and is crucial in accounting for forecast uncertainty in downscaling projects.

In the realm of particle physics, the tau lepton serves as an ideal bridge, linking the precise predictions of theoretical models with the meticulously conducted experimental studies. Its unique position enables the rigorous testing of two fundamental frameworks, the Standard Model and its accompanying quantum field theory as well as flavor physics, while also offering a distinctive window into the potential new physics that might exist beyond this model. With a well-measured mass and a relatively long lifespan, the tau lepton enables the calculation of intricate theoretical predictions to an astonishingly accurate extent of about 0.1%. This level of precision, combined with equally high experimental precision, makes any observed discrepancy with predictions a definitive indication of new underlying physics. This talk will review some of the most complex and demanding areas of tau lepton research, emphasizing the formidable challenges in achieving such remarkable precision, both in theoretical models and experimental investigations, particularly concerning off-shell effects and front-back asymmetries. With upcoming data from Belle II, to be complemented by data from Tomography@SPS, the prospects for making significant new discoveries in the near future are extremely promising.

Two large-scale rotating wavy chambers have been used to study the relationship between the rotation rates of their top and bottom sections and the impact of horizontal and vertical shears on the growth of unstable waves. By adjusting the rotation in each section, researchers created different types of wave instability: some influenced by horizontal shear and others by shear in the vertical direction. To understand how these factors affect the waves' behavior, two numerical models were used in conjunction with experimental data, and both produced accurate results for different scenarios. The outcomes of this study show that a specific type of numerical model, which considers the effects of fluid friction and wave motion while maintaining conservation of mass and energy, is particularly effective in predicting the behavior of waves in rotating systems and may be applicable to similar geophysical phenomena on Earth and other celestial bodies.

A novel parameterization of the exponential point process is presented, enabling efficient estimation using Markov chain Monte Carlo in the extreme value domain. This parameterization redefines a common exponential point process model with a location and shape parameter, often paired with an unknown threshold. By substituting the traditional scale parameter with an unknown inverse parameter, this reparameterization stays consistent with extreme value theory, albeit making scale a non-observable variable. We show that this substitution facilitates the direct sampling of the process's latent stochastic measure in the Bayesian framework, an advantage not seen with conventional model parameterizations which require computationally intensive methods like embedded Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for estimation. This new approach is evaluated using Bayesian model choice simulations and applied to a study of major European heatwaves between 1979 and 2018, yielding a 3-sigma temperature threshold estimate of 38.76°C for this period.

A significant hurdle in deploying reinforcement learning (RL) offline policies is the risk of online interference from non-RL agents utilizing different strategies. For instance, a retailer's offline-trained RL pricing model might be manipulated by competitors offering varying prices, thus shifting the reward system in ways the trained policy wasn't originally trained to handle. To overcome this obstacle, our study introduces a novel offline RL method that is resistant to fraud in diverse settings, employing a two-step process. Firstly, it uses fraud-resistant variational data augmentation to simulate how fraud could occur. Secondly, it trains the policy using this simulated data along with the original dataset. The resulting policy is demonstrated to be significantly more resilient when deployed online, especially in the retail pricing scenario, compared to standard RL techniques.

This study demonstrates the logarithmic convexity of the solution to the 1-D thermal equation under specific boundary conditions that dynamically change with space and time, and also changes impulsively in the process. The relevant logarithmic convexity function is defined over a specific domain within the longer section of the control domain. The control design uses a fundamental inequality derived from the system and the defined function to reach its goal, and the research also provides the maximum boundary force required for the impulsive control to be successful in its purpose. The outcome of this control design shows the ability to achieve a desired level of precision in controlling the system.

Many outside of the chosen training data can impact the performance of NLP tasks.
When encountering input that differs from the training data, a model may struggle to produce optimal results.
Consequently, many cutting-edge models are evaluated using a single metric from their best-performing scenarios.
However, this approach may obscure the potential of various models in different scenarios.
To effectively compare models, it is crucial to categorize external texts into distinct categories and make an accurate assessment of their potential.
Our study aims to shed light on outside of-domain texts by examining the potential sources of domain shifts.
We introduce four metrics to detect domain shifts and evaluate the effectiveness of existing approaches.
In addition, we offer cutting-edge methods for identifying domains shifts that surpass current state-of-the-art solutions by a significant margin.

In the realm of nanomachines, molecular engines, and quantum devices, understanding non-equilibrium processes, such as inelastic electron tunneling, is crucial. To address the complex dynamics arising from the interaction of electronic and molecular degrees of freedom, a theoretical framework has been developed using non-equilibrium Green's function and path integral techniques. This framework enables the application of fluctuation-dissipation theory and master equation formalism to explore key concepts, including energy tunneling fluctuations, mechanical fluctuations, and the breakdown of Fermi's golden rule. Notably, it has been demonstrated that non-equilibrium fluctuations can be harnessed to induce stochastic resonance in systems with a ratchet-like potential.

We are investigating the properties of Unilateral Resynchronizability for term transducers, specifically focusing on creating efficient algorithms to check this property and create corresponding bilateral transducers. In addition, we are exploring a stricter form of Unilateral Resynchronizability that can be reversed,称之为 Strict Unilateral Resynchronizability, and determining which scenarios allow a strict bilateral transducer to project onto its input.

This research note accelerates the process of calculating a specific function known as the m-fold generalized convolution for two discrete random variables, x and y. Utilizing precomputed values of the fast Fourier transform, the proposed method is significantly faster, requiring on the order of O(mn log n) time comparisons and cost operations, when compared to the standard approach's time complexity of O(mn log (mn)). To demonstrate the efficiency of this improvement, an actual implementation was provided in the form of open-source software and was used to calculate Born rule probabilities for up to ten intersecting lines on a grid with up to one million squares.

About two decades have passed since the initial detection of T-dwarfs, which are isolated from the main sequence due to their low luminosity, at a point where their internal heat is minimal and they are primarily powered by their formation energy.  The first confirmed t-dwarf, GJ 229B, has been the subject of extensive research through spectroscopy since its discovery.  Analyzing atmospheric features of cool brown dwarfs like GJ 229B is particularly difficult due to their complex atmospheric conditions and internal heat transfer.  The recent detection of CO absorption at 4.51 micrometers in GJ 229B, which contradicts model predictions, has been the subject of debate.  Applying a radiative transfer model to the near-infrared and mid-infrared spectra of GJ 229B, we have analyzed the CO absorption at 2.32 micrometers and discovered that it is located at a significantly deeper layer of the atmosphere than other CO and H2O absorption features, consistent with mid-energy type T-dwarfs like GJ 48B and GJ 176B.  The model also reveals that the atmospheric conditions at 4.51 micrometers are dominated by CO, which partially explains this unusual absorption feature detected by the MIRI instrument on the JWST.  The model's accuracy in predicting CO and H2O line depths has been verified with recent observations of

We examine the possibility of the $T_{cc}$ as a gluonic bound state, with the quantum numbers $J^{PC}=1^{++}$, and the $Y(4260)$ as a state with $J^{PC}=0^{--}$, utilizing QCD sum rules to investigate this hypothesis.

This discussion focuses on the LHCb experiment's role in measuring the LHCb's contribution to key parameters $\Delta a_2$ and $\Delta a_3$ in $B_s$ meson oscillations. We detail the LHCb data analysis method and evaluate current $\Delta a_2$ measurements in $B_s$ oscillations as well as estimates for $\Delta a_3$ from LHCb dataset accumulations up to 120 fb$^{-1}$ in integrated luminosity.

A researcher spread SARS-CoV-2 on a model of an urban bus by applying fluorescent spray to simulate transmission of an infectious agent via well-mixed droplets or aerosols. FluoAerosol, a type of fluorescent particle used for this purpose, was chosen due to its suitability for detecting low levels of transmission in experiments. Two methods were employed to collect the FluoAerosol and calculate its distribution throughout the bus: sampling on the bus model and numerical simulation using a computational fluid dynamics model. The results showed that an urban bus can be divided into two well-mixed zones when people are seated, with the floor area remaining relatively contamination-free due to low velocities and poor dispersion. However, contamination levels varied significantly depending on the bus layout and passenger configuration. These results support the use of a well-mixed approach for infectious disease transmission modeling in confined environments, such as buses, particularly when the spread of aerosols or droplets is involved.

Recent research on beta decay characteristics of heavy even-$N$ nuclei to odd neighbor states near the double-shell gap at $N=126$ led to a discovery of "prohibited" beta decays in $^{133}$Te. To better understand these features, similar studies were conducted on $^{135,137}$Te. Using a random shell model, a significant variation in the first forbidden (FF) $\beta^-$ decay of $^{135}$Te to $^{135}$I was found, with a 100-fold decrease, while no such large variation was observed in the first, second, or third forbidden ($\pi f_{7/2} \to \pi i_{13/2}$) $\beta^-$ decays of $^{135,137}$Te. Calculated log $ft$ values were in line with experimental data, and while theoretical results for the $\beta^-$ decay of $^{135,137}$Te matched the measured data, calculated log $ft$ values for $\beta^+$ or electron capture decays were significantly overestimated. Notably, both $\beta^+$ or electron capture decays of $^{135,137}$Te were found to be first forbidden.

Double-faced auctions serve as a reliable and efficient method to conduct public tenders, enabling the simultaneous purchase and sale of multiple items from diverse buyers and sellers. A particular type of double-faced auction, known as a simultaneous auction, conducts a single auction where only one bid round takes place. Due to a lack of established rules, simultaneous auctions have been largely unexplored until recently, when a validated, fair auction format was developed and accurately implemented in a computer program. This article presents a fair auction algorithm based on a previously published method, along with a thorough analysis of its underlying rationale and associated economics. As a use case, the validated algorithm has been successfully applied to organize a public tender for allocating airport slots, yielding results comparable to a private approach. The study also discusses the advantages of pursuing a public tender through simultaneous auctions.

Using heavy quark symmetry, we derive the mass formulae, transition form factors, and decay widths relevant to HQET analysis of HQSB decays, specifically focusing on $X(1P)$ baryons. Our study, which uses a set of eight light diquark operators, enables a systematic analysis of $|nS\rangle$, $|nP\rangle$, and bound state wave functions. This leads to detailed examinations of $F$-wave bottom baryons, including mass predictions and evaluations of mass differences and decay widths related to $HB(nP)\to\pi/ \eta/nK/ \rho/K(1400)$ transitions. Additionally, our study makes a comparison with available experimental data and provides a prediction for the LHCb to search for an $X(1P)$ state, which could correspond to the $\Omega_b(6291)$.

The concept of cyclic decomposition is introduced to break down problems involving nonexpansive curves into simpler components. A cyclic decomposition consists of cyclically equivalent configurations of nonexpansive curves. We establish that all cyclic decompositions of nonexpansive curves can be systematically identified. Furthermore, a novel approach based on an associated set of curves called shadow curves is developed to not only find all cyclic decompositions but also provide an measure of the minimal distortion between any nonexpansive curve and its closest symmetric counterpart. This concept of symmetry serves as a standardized form within each cyclic decomposition. It is also demonstrated that the number of cyclic decompositions of $d$-dimensional nonexpansive curves is at most $d!$. In three dimensions, an upper limit of $720$ is set for the number of cyclic decompositions. A cyclic decomposition of a problem can be utilized to simplify and reduce its complexity. We show that the problem complexity in $d$ dimensions does not exceed $d!/2^(⌊log_2(d)⌋) * (d mod 2)$.

This study delves into the connection between spectral decomposition methods and kernel machine learning to analyze the behavior of dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) in various linear and nonlinear disambiguation techniques. A new approach using kernel regression is proposed to derive an optimal DMD algorithm that is both accurate and versatile. By formulating a regression problem that captures the evolution of a phase space trajectory from a set of snapshots, a kernel can be employed to model this evolution in various scenarios. When a kernel machine is applied using a maximum likelihood framework, it naturally develops a Bayesian probabilistic interpretation for the resulting DMD algorithm. Furthermore, this approach offers a unified understanding of various DMD variants and provides a basis for developing new algorithms to handle resampling issues in dynamic mode decomposition. Consequently, a optimal kernel is selected to generate a data-driven approximation of the underlying system's operator that accurately and stably reconstructs the system's trajectory from available snapshot data.

This study examines the patterns of chess moves recurring frequently among grandmasters worldwide, particularly focusing on "book openings," which constitute approximately 40% of recorded games. Building upon earlier research, we used community-generated complexity ratings from "Chess.com," to analyze the intricated relationships between moves appearing often in established opening sequences, often forming a network structure. An algorithm was used to identify unique paths on this network representing standard opening sequences, and we verified the accuracy of these sequences by comparing them to those found in major chess opening databases. Additionally, we created a random chess move complexity model and assessed its impact on opening sequence on this network, and we found evidence of non-random patterns of move complexity influencing standard chess moves appearing often in established opening sequences, often forming a network structure.

This research derives a set of parameters for millisecond pulsars (PSPRs) in various white dwarves (WDs) by analyzing GPS data from the Five-year data release of the PSPR Timing Analysis Solution project. The parameters considered are the PSPR distance, the reduced love number of the WD, and the gravitational shift. An comparison is made of the effective and unrestricted models of three parameters in two degrees of freedom to determine the most relevant parameters. The results indicate that an effective model is attainable in certain circumstances. The studies are confined to PSPRs in metallic, dense, and magnetic WDs due to the prevailing timinansements in the NP data. The studies are made of two metallic, dense, and magnetic WDs: GP, which features four timing data, and the PSPR of the seven timing data.
